lessons.title: Where did it go?

steps.headline: Displacement is final position minus initial position, and its sign shows the direction.

lead.text: Position is measured from an origin, a place you choose to call zero. You also choose which way is positive.
A move to larger positions is positive. A move to smaller positions is negative.
The dot starts at 2 m and finishes at 9 m. Right is positive.

reveal.text: You just used final minus initial: 9 − 2. The plus sign says the dot moved the positive way.

steps.headline: Distance is the total length of the path, so every stretch adds.

lead.text: Displacement only compares the ends. Distance follows the whole path, and it counts the trip back as well as the trip out.
Distance has no direction and is never negative.

steps.headline: A trolley goes from 1 m to 5 m, then back to 2 m. Find its displacement and its distance.

workedSteps.text: Displacement uses only the ends: finish minus start.
Distance adds the stretches. Out is 5 − 1.
Back is 5 − 2. Add the two.

steps.headline: A cart goes from 1 m to 7 m and back to 1 m. What distance does it cover?

workedSteps.text: The way out runs from 1 m to 7 m.
The way back is the same length.
Add the two stretches.

lead.text: Two students watch the same trip. They measure from different origins, so their readings differ.

reveal.text: Moving the origin shifts both readings together. The gap between them is the displacement, and it stays put.

lead.text: A robot drives along a straight track, then turns round partway.

reveal.text: The robot's displacement is only +3 m, yet it covered 13 m. The turn makes the two numbers differ.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish a change in position from the total distance travelled.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You walk 5 m east from your front door, then turn and walk 2 m back west.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a change in position from the distance travelled, and give the change a sign.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later idea about motion starts from where things are and how that changes.

recap.keyIdea: Displacement is final position minus initial position, with a sign. Distance adds every stretch of the path.

blocks.text: You found that 5 m out and 2 m back leaves you 3 m from the door. You also saw an out-and-back trip of 6 m each way cover 12 m while ending where it began.

recap.nextHook: Now add time: how fast does the position change?

lessons.title: Speed and direction

steps.headline: Average speed is distance over time. Average velocity is displacement over time, so it has a sign.

lead.text: Both averages divide by the elapsed time. They differ in the top line: speed uses the distance travelled, velocity uses the displacement.
Speed is never negative. Velocity is negative when the move is in the negative direction.
A rover drives straight for 6 s and covers 18 m. It does not have to go at one pace the whole way.

reveal.text: You divided the distance by the time. That is an average: the rover may have been faster and slower along the way.

steps.headline: A trolley goes 15 m right in 3 s, then 5 m left in 2 s. Find both averages.

workedSteps.text: Add the distances and the times. Speed divides the first by the second.
Displacement is the net move, right positive.
Velocity divides the displacement by the same time.

steps.headline: A cart's displacement is −12 m over 3 s. What is its average velocity?

workedSteps.text: The displacement is negative, so the cart moved left.
The elapsed time is positive.
Divide the displacement by the time.

lead.text: A runner goes out 10 m from a marker and comes straight back to it. Think about where the runner ends up.

reveal.text: The finish equals the start, so the displacement is zero. Distance and displacement part company on a return trip.

lead.text: A robot covers two equal stretches, but the second takes longer than the first.

reveal.text: The whole trip is 12 m in 6 s. The mean of the two stretch speeds is 2.25 m/s, which overweights the faster stretch.

lessons.orientation: Use elapsed time to distinguish average speed from average velocity.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You cycle at a steady pace and cover 20 m in 4 s.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find average speed and average velocity from a trip, and say when they differ.

recap.keyIdea: Average speed is total distance over time. Average velocity is displacement over time, so it carries a sign and is zero on a return trip.

blocks.text: You turned 20 m in 4 s into 5 m each second. You then found that a return trip has average velocity 0 even though the runner covered 20 m.

recap.nextHook: Draw it: how does a position–time graph show speed and direction?

lessons.title: Read a motion graph

steps.headline: On a position–time graph, the slope is the velocity.

lead.text: Time runs along the horizontal axis and position up the vertical one. A straight segment rises or falls by the same amount each second.
A steeper line means a faster move. A falling line means a negative velocity.
The line runs from 2 m at 0 s up to 14 m at 3 s.

reveal.text: You divided the rise by the run. That quotient is the velocity along the segment.

steps.headline: Read the graph: out for 2 s, stop for 2 s, then back.

workedSteps.text: The first stretch rises from 0 m to 8 m in 2 s.
The middle stretch is flat, so the position holds.
The last stretch falls from 8 m to 2 m in 2 s.

steps.headline: Read the graph between 2 s and 4 s, where the line is level.

workedSteps.text: The position at 2 s is 8 m.
The position at 4 s is also 8 m.
What does the object do?

lead.text: This segment falls from left to right. Think about what a falling position means for the direction of motion.

reveal.text: Final minus initial is negative, so the velocity is negative: motion in the negative direction.

lead.text: A graph shows a trip with a pause and a turn. Only the start, the finish and the total time matter for the average.

reveal.text: The pause and the turn still use up time, so they pull the average velocity down to 1/3 m/s.

lessons.orientation: Interpret a position–time graph as changing position, pauses and reversals.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A friend walks steadily away from you. After 2 s they are 3 m away.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read velocity from the slope of a position–time graph and spot pauses and turns.

recap.keyIdea: On a position–time graph, slope is velocity: steep is fast, flat is stopped and falling is negative. Average velocity uses the endpoints.

blocks.text: You turned 3 m after 2 s into 9 m after 6 s, and read a pause as a flat line. Over a trip with a pause and a turn you found an average velocity of just 1/3 m/s.

recap.nextHook: When velocity itself changes, how fast does it change?

lessons.title: Changing velocity

steps.headline: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time it takes.

lead.text: Velocity can change in size, in direction or both. Acceleration measures how quickly.
The unit is m/s², metres per second, every second.
A cart's velocity rises from 2 m/s to 10 m/s over 4 s.

reveal.text: You divided the change in velocity by the time. Equal time steps add equal velocity changes when acceleration is constant.

steps.headline: A cart moving left goes from −8 m/s to −2 m/s in 3 s. Find its acceleration.

workedSteps.text: Change in velocity is final minus initial. Subtracting −8 adds 8.
The velocity went up towards zero, so the change is positive.
Divide by the time.

steps.headline: Velocity goes from −8 m/s to −2 m/s over 3 s. What is the acceleration?

workedSteps.text: Final velocity minus initial velocity.
Divide by the elapsed time.

lead.text: A cart moves left and its acceleration also points left. Compare the two directions.

reveal.text: Same direction means speeding up. The minus sign does not decide it; the comparison does.

lead.text: A cart holds 6 m/s for 4 s. It keeps moving the whole time.

reveal.text: Velocity did not change, so acceleration is zero, yet the position keeps changing.

lessons.orientation: Read acceleration as a signed change in velocity per second.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A car rolls at 10 m/s and picks up 3 m/s every second.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find acceleration from a change in velocity and read its sign.

recap.keyIdea: Acceleration is change in velocity over time. Its sign comes from final minus initial velocity, and speeding up or slowing down depends on how it compares with velocity.

blocks.text: You found a car at 10 m/s reach 22 m/s after 4 s of 3 m/s². You also showed a cart going from −8 to −2 m/s has positive acceleration while it slows.

recap.nextHook: Put velocity and acceleration together to predict where a cart will be.

lessons.title: Predict the next position

steps.headline: With constant acceleration, final velocity is initial velocity plus acceleration times time.

lead.text: Constant acceleration means the velocity changes by the same amount every second. Write u for the starting velocity, a for the acceleration and t for the time.
A negative a takes velocity away each second.
A cart starts at 3 m/s and accelerates at a steady 2 m/s². Look at how long it runs.

reveal.text: You added the velocity gained each second to the starting velocity: 3 + 2 × 4.

steps.headline: A cart starts at 2 m/s and accelerates at 1 m/s² for 6 s. How far does it go?

workedSteps.text: Find the final velocity.
Average the start and the finish.
Distance is average velocity times time.

steps.headline: A cart starts at 3 m/s and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 4 s. How far does it go?

workedSteps.text: The final velocity is 3 + 2 × 4.
The average of the start and finish.
Multiply the average velocity by the time.

lead.text: Brakes can be treated as a constant acceleration. A cart slows steadily until it stops.

reveal.text: Same method: the average of 12 and 0 is 6 m/s, and that applies for the whole 4 s.

lead.text: Now the cart starts from rest and speeds up steadily. Compare the same cart after one time and after twice that time.

reveal.text: Doubling the time doubles the final velocity and the average, so the distance grows fourfold.

lessons.orientation: Use a constant acceleration to predict velocity and displacement.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A train moves at a steady 5 m/s for 8 s.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict the velocity and the displacement of a cart that accelerates at a constant rate.

recap.keyIdea: With constant acceleration, v = u + at, and displacement is the average of the start and finish velocities times the time.

blocks.text: You found a train at 5 m/s covers 40 m in 8 s, then used the average of two velocities to find how far a cart travels while it speeds up or brakes.

recap.nextHook: Gravity is a constant acceleration too. What does it do to a ball?

lessons.title: Falling and rising

steps.headline: In free fall, everything accelerates at 10 m/s² downward, whatever its mass.

lead.text: Free fall means gravity is the only force acting. Here that means no air resistance.
Choose upward as positive and the acceleration is −10 m/s². The sign tells you the direction, nothing else.
Rising, at the top and falling: the acceleration is the same.
A ball is released from rest. Upward is positive.

reveal.text: You used v = u + at with a = −10. A negative velocity means the ball moves downward.

steps.headline: A ball is dropped from 80 m. How high is it after 3 s?

workedSteps.text: The distance fallen is ½gt².
The ball moves down, so its displacement is negative.
Add the displacement to the starting height.

steps.headline: A ball is dropped from 45 m. How high is it after 2 s?

workedSteps.text: The distance fallen in 2 s is ½gt².
Take that fall off the starting height of 45 m.

lead.text: Throw a ball straight up. It slows, stops for an instant at the top, then drops back.

reveal.text: The velocity is zero at the top but the acceleration is not. Gravity gave −10 on the way up and gives −10 now.

lead.text: Two balls of different mass leave the same height at the same moment. Air resistance is ignored.

reveal.text: Mass cancels: a heavier ball is pulled harder but also has more to move. Free fall is the same for both.

lessons.orientation: Apply constant downward acceleration to free fall and an upward throw.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A dropped stone speeds up by 10 m/s every second it falls.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict the velocity and height of a falling or thrown ball, and say what gravity does at the top.

recap.keyIdea: Free fall has one constant acceleration, 10 m/s² downward, whether the object rises, falls or sits at the top. Mass does not change it.

blocks.text: You found a stone gains 50 m/s in 5 s at 10 m/s each second. You also saw that a ball's velocity is zero at the top of a throw while its acceleration is still −10 m/s².

recap.nextHook: What do forces do to an object that is not accelerating?

lessons.title: When forces balance

steps.headline: The net force is the sum of the forces on one object, with a sign for direction.

lead.text: Pick the object first. Then give each force a sign: positive if it points the way you chose as positive, negative if it points the other way.
Forces are balanced when the net force is zero. Then the velocity does not change.
Two horizontal forces act on a cart. One points right and one points left. Right is positive.

reveal.text: You gave the leftward force a minus sign and added: 14 − 6. The sum points right, so it is positive.

steps.headline: A sled has forces of 12 N right, 7 N left and 3 N left. Find the net force.

workedSteps.text: Give each force its sign, rightward positive.
Add them.
The result is small and positive, so the sled's net push is slightly to the right.

steps.headline: A resting cart has 9 N right and 9 N left on it. What is the net force?

workedSteps.text: The rightward force counts as positive.
The leftward force counts as negative.
Add them.

lead.text: A cart rolls right at 3 m/s. The forces on it add up to zero.

reveal.text: Zero net force means no change in velocity, so the cart keeps its 3 m/s. It needs no push to keep going.

lead.text: A cart rolls right, but the bigger force on it points left.

reveal.text: The net force points left while the cart still moves right. The force changes the velocity; it does not show where the cart is going.

lessons.orientation: Add signed forces and distinguish balanced forces from being at rest.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: In a tug of war, one team pulls left with 400 N and the other pulls right with 350 N.

intro.promise: By the end you'll add forces with signs, and say what balanced forces do to an object's velocity.

recap.keyIdea: The net force is the signed sum of the forces on one object. When it is zero, the velocity does not change.

blocks.text: You found that a 400 N pull and a 350 N pull leave 50 N over. You also saw a cart with balanced forces keep rolling at 3 m/s.

recap.nextHook: If forces do not balance, how much does the velocity change?

lessons.title: Force, mass and acceleration

steps.headline: Newton's second law: the net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration.

lead.text: The same net force gives a small mass a big acceleration and a large mass a small one. The acceleration points the way the net force points.
Use the net force, not just one of the forces.
A 3 kg cart has two horizontal forces on it, one pointing right and one pointing left. Right is positive.

reveal.text: You found the net force first, then divided by the mass. That is the second law at work.

steps.headline: A trolley of mass 8 kg has 30 N right and 6 N left on it. Find its acceleration.

workedSteps.text: Find the net force. The leftward force is negative.
Divide the net force by the mass.
The sign is positive, so the acceleration points right.

steps.headline: A net force of 24 N pushes a 2 kg cart to the right. Find its acceleration.

workedSteps.text: The force given is already the net force.
The mass is 2 kg.
Divide the net force by the mass.

lead.text: A 4 kg cart moves right at 6 m/s. A 4 N force pushes it right and a 12 N force pushes it left.

reveal.text: The acceleration follows the net force, not the motion. The cart is still going right, but it is slowing down.

lead.text: Keep the net force the same and swap the cart for one with twice the mass.

reveal.text: a = F ÷ m, so doubling m halves a. Heavier objects respond less to the same force.

lessons.orientation: Use net force and mass to predict how velocity changes.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The same push speeds an empty trolley up by 6 m/s every second.

intro.promise: By the end you'll use net force and mass to find acceleration, and the other way round.

recap.keyIdea: The net force equals mass times acceleration: more force, more acceleration; more mass, less. The acceleration points the way the net force points.

blocks.text: You saw the same push on twice the mass give 3 m/s², half of 6. You also found that a cart moving right can accelerate left when the net force points that way.

recap.nextHook: Why do some forces, like weight, seem to do nothing? Something is pushing back.

lessons.title: Weight and support

steps.headline: Weight is the gravitational force on an object, W = mg. Mass stays the same wherever you go.

lead.text: Mass is measured in kilograms and belongs to the object. Weight is a force in newtons that depends on g.
On a planet with a different g, the weight changes. The mass does not.
An object has a mass of 3 kg in a place where g is 10 m/s².

reveal.text: You multiplied mass by g. The result is a force in newtons, not a mass in kilograms.

steps.headline: A support pushes up on an object. At rest it equals the weight; accelerating upward it is bigger.

lead.text: The support force acts upward on an object resting on a surface or carried in a lift. Take upward as positive: the net force is the support force minus the weight.
At rest, a = 0, so N = mg.

steps.headline: A 2 kg load is carried upward at 3 m/s² in a lift. Find the support force. Take g as 10 m/s².

workedSteps.text: The weight is mg.
The net upward force must give the acceleration.
The support force carries the weight and supplies the net force.

steps.headline: A 4 kg object is accelerated upward at 2 m/s². Find the support force with g = 10 m/s².

workedSteps.text: The weight is mg.
The extra force for the acceleration is ma.
Add them to find the support force.

lead.text: A 4 kg object rests on a horizontal support. Only weight and the support force act.

reveal.text: No acceleration means the two forces cancel. The support force has exactly the size of the weight.

lead.text: Carry the same object to a place with a weaker gravitational field.

reveal.text: Weight falls with g, but the mass is the same amount of matter. Mass is not weight.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish mass, gravitational force and the force from a support.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Gravity pulls on every kilogram with a force of 10 N.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell mass from weight, and find the support force on an object at rest or accelerating.

recap.keyIdea: Weight is mg and changes with g; mass does not. A support force balances the weight at rest and exceeds it when the object accelerates upward.

blocks.text: You found a 6 kg bag is pulled with 60 N. You also found a 4 kg object needs 40 N of support at rest and 48 N when accelerating upward at 2 m/s².

recap.nextHook: Forces come in pairs. What is the partner of the support force?

lessons.title: Forces come in pairs

steps.headline: Newton's third law: if A pushes B, B pushes A with an equal force in the opposite direction.

lead.text: The two forces make a pair. They are equal in size and opposite in direction, and they act on different objects.
Because each acts on a different object, a pair never cancels on either one.
Cart B pushes cart A to the left with a force of 10 N.

reveal.text: A pushes B with the same 10 N, directed right. The pair is equal in size and opposite in direction.

steps.headline: A 3 kg cart A and a 6 kg cart B push apart with 12 N each. Find both accelerations.

workedSteps.text: B feels A's push to the right. Divide by B's mass.
A feels B's push to the left. Divide by A's mass.
The lighter cart accelerates more, in the opposite direction.

steps.headline: Cart A pushes a 5 kg cart B right with 10 N. Find B's acceleration.

workedSteps.text: The force on B is A's push, to the right.
B's mass is 5 kg.
Divide the force on B by B's mass.

lead.text: Now look at the other cart. Cart A has mass 2 kg, and its only horizontal force is B's leftward push of 10 N. Right is positive.

reveal.text: The same size of force gave a bigger acceleration, because A has less mass.

lead.text: Now treat the two carts as one system. Their pair of forces is inside it.

reveal.text: Inside one system the pair cancels, so it cannot change the system's overall motion. Each cart still accelerates because the pair acts on it alone.

lessons.orientation: Identify an interaction pair and explain why equal forces can produce different accelerations.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Skater A pushes skater B with a force of 40 N.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the partner of any force, and say why equal forces can still give different accelerations.

recap.keyIdea: Forces come in pairs, equal and opposite, on different objects. Equal forces give different accelerations when the masses differ.

blocks.text: You found that B pushes back on A with 40 N, and that a 3 kg cart and a 6 kg cart pushed apart by 12 N accelerate at 4 and 2 m/s² in opposite directions.

recap.nextHook: Surfaces push back along them as well. How does friction decide whether a box slides?

lessons.title: Friction that adjusts

steps.headline: Static friction matches the push up to a limit. Once the box slides, friction has a fixed size.

lead.text: On a level surface the support force is mg. Static friction can be as large as μs times that, and no larger. Sliding friction is μk times it.
Below the limit, static friction equals the push, not the limit.
A 4 kg box can hold at most 20 N of static friction. You push it with 12 N and it stays put.

reveal.text: Friction matched your push, 12 N. The 20 N is only the ceiling, not what friction supplies.

steps.headline: A 3 kg crate has μs = 0.4. It is pushed with 15 N on a level floor. Does it slide? Use g = 10 m/s².

workedSteps.text: The support force equals the weight.
The most static friction the floor can give.
The 15 N push beats the 12 N limit, so the crate slides.

steps.headline: A 4 kg box has μs = 0.5. What is the most static friction it can get, with g = 10 m/s²?

workedSteps.text: The support force equals the weight.
Multiply by the static coefficient.

lead.text: The box now slides. Use the sliding coefficient this time. The support force is still mg.

reveal.text: Sliding friction is fixed by the coefficient and the support force. It does not grow with the push.

lead.text: A sliding 4 kg box is pushed right with 24 N while sliding friction pulls left.

reveal.text: Net force is push minus friction. That is what accelerates the box: 12 N on 4 kg.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish static and sliding friction, and predict whether a push moves a box.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A heavy crate does not budge when you push it with 30 N.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say how much friction holds a box, and whether a push will make it slide.

recap.keyIdea: Static friction matches the push up to a limit of μs times the support force. Sliding friction is μk times that, and the net force comes from push minus friction.

blocks.text: You found that friction cancelled your 30 N push on a crate that did not move, and that a 15 N push beats a 12 N limit. For a sliding 4 kg box you found an acceleration of 3 m/s².

recap.nextHook: When a force moves something, it does work. How do we measure that?

lessons.title: When a force does work

steps.headline: A force does work when it acts along a displacement: work is force times distance, in joules.

lead.text: Work links a force to a move. Push along the movement and the work is positive. Push against it and the work is negative.
One joule is one newton acting over one metre.
A constant 15 N force acts along a 4 m displacement.

reveal.text: You multiplied force by distance, so the work is positive: the force acts along the move.

steps.headline: A box slides 3 m while an 8 N friction force acts against it. Find the work done by friction.

workedSteps.text: Friction points against the displacement, so its work is negative.
Multiply force by distance.
Attach the sign.

steps.headline: A 6 N force acts opposite to a 5 m displacement. Find its work.

workedSteps.text: The force opposes the move, so the work is negative.
Multiply the force by the distance, with the sign.

lead.text: Only the part of a force along the displacement does work. A vertical support force acts while the box slides horizontally.

reveal.text: The support force has no part along the move, so its work is zero.

lead.text: Several forces may act on a cart. Work is found for one force at a time.

reveal.text: This pull does 70 J. A separate opposing 4 N force over the same 7 m would do −28 J.

lessons.orientation: Calculate signed work for forces along, against and perpendicular to displacement.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Pushing a box 2 m with a steady push costs 20 units of effort.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the work done by a force along, against or across a movement.

recap.keyIdea: A force does work Fd when it acts along a displacement: positive along, negative against and zero at right angles. Net work is the signed sum.

blocks.text: You saw that pushing 2 m costs 20 units, so 8 m costs 80. You found a 15 N force over 4 m does 60 J, and a 6 N force against 5 m does −30 J.

recap.nextHook: Work changes something. What does a force do to a moving object's energy?

lessons.title: Energy of motion

steps.headline: Kinetic energy is ½mv²: the energy a moving object has because of its speed.

lead.text: Kinetic energy depends on the mass and on the square of the speed. It is never negative, and it does not depend on direction.
The unit is the joule.
A 2 kg cart moves at 3 m/s.

reveal.text: You squared the speed, multiplied by the mass and halved it: ½ × 2 × 9 gives 9 J.

steps.headline: A 1 kg ball speeds up from 2 m/s to 4 m/s. Compare its kinetic energies.

workedSteps.text: Kinetic energy at 2 m/s.
Kinetic energy at 4 m/s.
Divide the new energy by the old.

steps.headline: A cart's speed doubles and its mass stays the same. By what factor does the kinetic energy change?

workedSteps.text: Mass is fixed, so only v² can change.
Replace v with 2v and square it.

steps.headline: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.

lead.text: A net force that speeds an object up does positive net work. One that slows it down does negative net work.
A 2 kg cart is pushed until it goes faster. Find the energy at each speed first.

reveal.text: Net work is the gain in kinetic energy, from 9 J to 25 J.

lead.text: Keep the speed fixed and change the mass instead.

reveal.text: Mass enters ½mv² once, so energy scales with mass directly. Speed is the term that is squared.

lessons.orientation: Use kinetic energy and net work to connect force with a change in speed.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Brakes stop a bike from 3 m/s in 1 m.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find kinetic energy and see how net work changes it.

recap.keyIdea: Kinetic energy is ½mv², so it grows with the square of the speed. Net work equals the change in kinetic energy.

blocks.text: You found that a bike at twice the speed needs four times the stopping distance, and that speeding a 2 kg cart from 3 m/s to 5 m/s takes 16 J of net work.

recap.nextHook: Height stores energy too. How much?

lessons.title: Energy and height

steps.headline: Raising an object stores gravitational potential energy: ΔU = mgΔh.

lead.text: Lifting takes work against gravity, and that work is stored. Δh is the final height minus the initial height, so a fall gives a negative change.
A 3 kg object is raised from 1 m to 5 m. Take g as 10 m/s².

reveal.text: You found the height change first, then multiplied by mg: 4 m of rise gave 120 J.

steps.headline: A 4 kg object falls from 9 m to 2 m with g = 10 m/s². Find its potential-energy change.

workedSteps.text: The height change is final minus initial.
The weight is mg.
Multiply the weight by the height change.

steps.headline: A 2 kg object descends from 8 m to 3 m with g = 10 m/s². Find its potential-energy change.

workedSteps.text: The height change is final minus initial.
Multiply mass, g and the height change.

steps.headline: The work gravity does is minus the change in potential energy.

lead.text: Gravity pulls down. When an object goes down, gravity helps the movement and does positive work. When it goes up, gravity opposes it and does negative work.
The same 2 kg object descends from 8 m to 3 m. Use the sign of the energy change you found.

reveal.text: A fall lowers potential energy by 100 J, so gravity did +100 J of work.

lead.text: Two people describe the same rise. One measures height from the floor, the other from the table.

reveal.text: Both readings of height shift together, so the difference, and the energy change, agree.

lessons.orientation: Calculate gravitational potential-energy changes using a chosen height reference.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You lift a 4 kg box slowly onto a shelf 2 m higher.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the potential energy a height change stores, and the work gravity does.

recap.keyIdea: Raising an object by Δh stores mgΔh of potential energy. Gravity's work is the opposite sign of that change, and the reference height does not matter.

blocks.text: You found a 4 kg box lifted 2 m takes 80 J. You also found a 2 kg object falling 5 m loses 100 J of potential energy while gravity does +100 J.

recap.nextHook: Where does lost potential energy go? Follow the energy through a descent.

lessons.title: Where the energy goes

steps.headline: Energy changes form but the total of every form stays fixed.

lead.text: Count the object, Earth and the surface as one system. As an object descends, potential energy falls. It becomes kinetic energy and, with friction, thermal energy.
A 2 kg object starts from rest at a height of 10 m with g = 10 m/s². Nothing but gravity does work.

reveal.text: All the potential energy lost, 2 × 10 × 10, became kinetic energy.

steps.headline: A 2 kg block slides down from 4 m with g = 10 m/s². 30 J becomes heating. Find its final kinetic energy.

workedSteps.text: Potential energy lost.
Some of it heats the surface.
The rest becomes kinetic energy.

steps.headline: A 2 kg object drops from 10 m with g = 10 m/s². 40 J becomes heating. Find the final kinetic energy.

workedSteps.text: Potential energy lost.
Take off the thermal energy.

steps.headline: Kinetic energy gives speed through v = √(2K/m).

lead.text: Once you know the final kinetic energy, rearrange K = ½mv² to find how fast the object moves.
A 2 kg object ends a descent with some kinetic energy. Work out its speed.

reveal.text: With 100 J and 2 kg, v² is 100 and v is 10 m/s.

lead.text: An object slides down a rough track. The object, Earth and track are one system with nothing else acting on it.

reveal.text: Include the heating and the books balance: kinetic plus potential plus thermal never changes.

lessons.orientation: Account for motion, height and heating during a descent.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A 1 kg ball held 5 m up has 50 J of stored energy.

intro.promise: By the end you'll balance the energy account of a descent, with or without heating.

recap.keyIdea: Energy is never lost: potential energy becomes kinetic and thermal energy, and the total of every form stays fixed.

blocks.text: You found that a 50 J ball lands with 50 J of motion when nothing else takes energy, and that 30 J of heating leaves a sliding block with 50 J out of 80 J.

recap.nextHook: How quickly is energy moving, and how much of it does the job?

lessons.title: Power and efficiency

steps.headline: Power is energy transferred per second. One watt is one joule per second.

lead.text: Power says how fast energy is moving, not how much. The same energy delivered in less time is more power.
A device delivers 1,200 J of useful energy in 4 s.

reveal.text: You divided the energy by the time: 1,200 ÷ 4 gives 300 joules each second, 300 W.

steps.headline: Efficiency is the useful output energy divided by the input energy.

lead.text: Not all the input does the job you want. The rest leaves as heat, sound or similar. Efficiency is the useful share.

steps.headline: A motor takes in 500 J and delivers 400 J of useful output. Find its efficiency and the wasted energy.

workedSteps.text: Useful output over input.
The rest leaves through other outputs.

steps.headline: A device takes in 2,000 J and delivers 1,200 J of useful output. Find its efficiency.

workedSteps.text: Divide useful output by input.
Turn the fraction into a percentage.

lead.text: The same device stores no net energy. Everything that is not useful output must leave another way.

reveal.text: The input of 2,000 J less the 1,200 J of useful output leaves 800 J as heat, sound or similar.

lead.text: A machine now delivers the same useful energy as before, but in half the time.

reveal.text: Power doubles because the same energy takes half as long. The efficiency has not been shown to change.

lessons.orientation: Separate energy transferred, transfer rate and the fraction reaching a useful output.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A motor uses 600 J of energy in 3 s.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find power from energy and time, and efficiency from useful output and input.

recap.keyIdea: Power is energy per second and efficiency is the useful share of the input. They measure different things: how fast, and how much of it is useful.

blocks.text: You found that 600 J in 3 s is 200 J each second. You also found 1,200 J of useful output from 2,000 J input is 60% efficient, with 800 J going elsewhere.

recap.nextHook: Now track motion itself: how do forces over time change it?

lessons.title: Momentum and impulse

steps.headline: Momentum is mass times velocity, and its sign shows the direction.

lead.text: A heavy or fast object has a lot of momentum. Unlike kinetic energy, momentum can be negative: it follows the sign of the velocity.
A 3 kg cart moves right at 4 m/s. Right is positive.

reveal.text: You multiplied the mass by the signed velocity. The plus sign comes from the direction of motion.

steps.headline: Impulse is force times time, and it equals the change in momentum.

lead.text: A net force acting for a time changes the momentum. The product is called impulse.

steps.headline: A 2 kg cart moves at +3 m/s. A 5 N net force acts for 4 s. Find its final velocity.

workedSteps.text: Initial momentum.
Impulse is force times time. Add it to the momentum.
Divide by the mass.

steps.headline: A 3 kg cart moves at +4 m/s. A net impulse of +18 N·s acts. Find its final velocity.

workedSteps.text: Initial momentum.
Add the impulse.
Divide by the mass.

lead.text: A 2 kg cart moves right and a negative impulse acts on it. Keep the sign when you add it to the momentum.

reveal.text: A negative impulse subtracted momentum, so the cart slowed but kept moving right.

lead.text: A 2 kg cart reverses from +4 m/s to −4 m/s. Compare what changes and what does not.

reveal.text: Speed squared is the same, so kinetic energy is too. Momentum changes by −16 kg·m/s because it carries the sign.

lessons.orientation: Track signed momentum and use force acting over time to predict its change.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Stopping a ball takes a steady 40 N for 0.5 s.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find momentum and impulse, and use them to find a final velocity or an average force.

recap.keyIdea: Momentum is mass times velocity and carries a sign. Impulse, force times time, equals the change in momentum.

blocks.text: You saw that stopping a ball over four times as long takes a quarter of the force. You also found that a 2 kg cart reversing from +4 to −4 m/s keeps its kinetic energy but flips its momentum.

recap.nextHook: When two carts collide, whose momentum changes? Both, by the same amount.

lessons.title: When carts stick together

steps.headline: When carts stick, total momentum is conserved and the carts share one velocity.

lead.text: Add each cart's momentum, mass times signed velocity. Afterwards the two masses move together.
This holds when the external impulse on the two carts is negligible.
A 2 kg cart at +6 m/s hits a resting 4 kg cart and they stick.

reveal.text: You added the momenta to get 12 kg·m/s, then divided by the combined mass.

steps.headline: A 3 kg cart at +4 m/s and a 1 kg cart at −8 m/s collide and stick. Find their shared velocity.

workedSteps.text: Momentum of the first cart.
Momentum of the second cart.
Add them and divide by the total mass.

steps.headline: A 2 kg cart at +6 m/s and a 4 kg cart at −3 m/s collide and stick. Find their shared velocity.

workedSteps.text: Momentum of the first cart.
Momentum of the second cart.
Add them and divide by the total mass.

steps.headline: A sticking collision conserves momentum but not kinetic energy.

lead.text: Some kinetic energy becomes deformation, heat and sound. A collision like this is called inelastic.
Momentum before equals momentum after. Kinetic energy afterwards is less.
A 2 kg cart at 6 m/s hits a resting 4 kg cart. They stick and move at 2 m/s. Find the kinetic energy before and after.

reveal.text: From 36 J to 12 J: two thirds of the kinetic energy became other forms, yet momentum was conserved.

lead.text: Forces between the carts during the crash are internal to the system. Other forces could act from outside.

reveal.text: Internal forces cancel in the total, so only a significant external impulse could change it.

lessons.orientation: Conserve signed momentum across a sticking collision and account for the kinetic-energy change.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: An 8 m/s cart runs into an identical cart at rest, and the two lock together.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the speed of carts that stick, and say what happens to their kinetic energy.

recap.keyIdea: When carts stick, total momentum is conserved and found with signs; the shared velocity is that momentum over the combined mass, and some kinetic energy is lost.

blocks.text: You saw identical carts halve the speed of a moving cart. You also found that a 2 kg cart and a 4 kg cart moving at opposite velocities can stop each other completely.

recap.nextHook: You now have the tools for motion, force and energy.

questions.prompt: An object moves from x = 2 m to x = 9 m. With right positive, what is its displacement in metres?
hints: Locate the starting and finishing coordinates.
Subtract the start from the finish.
Calculate 9 − 2.
questions.onCorrect: +7 m. Final minus initial: the size is how far it moved and the plus sign says which way.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two readings. Displacement is a difference: final minus initial.
The size is right, but the sign is not. It moved towards larger positions.

questions.prompt: A cart goes from 1 m to 7 m and back to 1 m. What total distance does it travel, in metres?
hints: Count both stretches of the trip.
Each stretch has length 7 − 1 metres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It travels 6 m out and 6 m back, for 12 m.

questions.onCorrect: 12 m. Distance adds every stretch of the path, so the trip back counts as well as the trip out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how far the cart ended from where it began. Distance counts every stretch it travelled.
That is the trip out only. The cart also has to come back.

questions.prompt: The origin shifts so that a trip from 2 m to 9 m is recorded as 12 m to 19 m. What happens to the displacement?
hints: Compare the differences between the two pairs of endpoints.

acceptedIdeas: It stays the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both readings increase by 10 m; their difference stays +7 m.

questions.onCorrect: It stays the same. Both readings rise by the same amount, so their difference does not change.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the readings change, not the trip. Both ends move by the same amount, so the gap between them does not grow.
Nothing in the trip doubled. Compare the gap between the two readings in each pair.

questions.prompt: A robot moves from 0 m to 8 m, then back to 3 m. How far does it travel altogether, in metres?
hints: Break the trip at the turning point.
The return stretch runs from 8 m to 3 m.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The path has lengths 8 m and 5 m: 8 + 5 = 13 m.

questions.onCorrect: 13 m. Break the trip at the turning point and add the two stretches.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how far the robot ended from where it began. The distance counts the whole path.
That is the trip out only. The robot also travels back.
That is the return stretch only. Count the trip out as well.

questions.prompt: A lift's marked position changes from 5 m to −4 m. With upward positive, find its displacement in metres.
hints: Keep the minus sign on the final position.
Subtract the initial position from the final position.
Calculate −4 − 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Final minus initial gives −4 − 5 = −9 m, downward.

questions.onCorrect: −9 m. Final minus initial gives a negative number when the move is in the negative direction.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the lift went down. With upward positive, a downward move needs a minus sign.
That adds the two readings. Take the start away from the finish.

questions.prompt: A cart travels from −2 m to 4 m and then to 1 m. Which statement describes its trip?
hints: Use endpoints for displacement and both path lengths for distance.

acceptedIdeas: Displacement 3 m; distance 9 m
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its displacement is 1 − (−2) = 3 m. Its distance is 6 + 3 = 9 m.

questions.onCorrect: Displacement compares the ends: 3 m. Distance adds both stretches: 9 m.

misconceptions.feedback: These are swapped. The ends give the displacement, and the whole path gives the distance.
The cart finishes at a larger position than it started, so its displacement is not negative.

questions.prompt: A rover covers 18 m in 6 s without reversing. What is its average speed in m/s?
hints: Use total distance and elapsed time.
Divide distance by time.
Share the travelled distance equally across the elapsed seconds.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s. Average speed is total distance divided by total time.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the distance by the time. Speed is distance shared out over time, so divide.
That divides time by distance. Speed is distance per unit of time.

questions.prompt: A cart's displacement is −12 m over 3 s. Find its average velocity in m/s.
hints: Velocity keeps the direction of displacement.
Divide the signed displacement by elapsed time.
Divide the displacement magnitude by duration and keep its negative sign.
questions.onCorrect: −4 m/s. Velocity keeps the sign of the displacement, so a leftward move gives a negative velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the cart moved left. Velocity keeps the sign of the displacement.
That multiplies by the time. Divide the displacement by it.

questions.prompt: A runner goes 10 m from a marker and returns to that marker in a total of 5 s. Find the average velocity in m/s.
hints: Use the final and initial positions.
A return to the same point leaves no displacement.
Divide that displacement by the total time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The displacement is zero, so average velocity is 0/5 = 0 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: 0 m/s. The runner ends where they began, so the displacement is zero whatever the distance run.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the average speed for the out leg only. Velocity uses the displacement over the whole trip.
That divides the distance there and back by the time. Velocity uses displacement, not distance.

questions.prompt: A robot travels 6 m in 2 s, then 6 m in 4 s. What is its average speed for the whole trip?
hints: Combine distances and times before dividing.

acceptedIdeas: 2 m/s
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The whole trip is 12 m in 6 s, giving 2 m/s. The slower section lasts longer.

questions.onCorrect: 2 m/s. Add the distances, add the times, then divide. Averaging the two speeds would over-weight the fast stretch.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean of the two stretch speeds. The slower stretch lasts longer, so it should count for more.
That is the speed of the first stretch only. Use the whole trip.

questions.prompt: A conveyor moves a parcel 42 m along a straight path in 7 s. What is its average speed in m/s?
hints: Identify the path length and duration.
Use distance divided by time.
Find how many metres correspond to one second.
questions.onCorrect: 6 m/s. Distance divided by time, with the path length and the duration both read from the problem.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two numbers. Divide the distance by the time.
That divides time by distance. Speed is distance per second.

questions.prompt: A moving object returns to its start. Which average must be zero over the complete trip?
hints: Ask which average uses displacement.

acceptedIdeas: Average velocity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only average velocity must be zero, because displacement is zero. The distance travelled is positive.

questions.onCorrect: Average velocity. A return to the start makes the displacement zero; the distance travelled stays positive.

misconceptions.feedback: Average speed uses distance, and the distance run is not zero. Which average uses displacement?
Only one of them uses displacement. The other uses the distance, which cannot be zero for a trip.

questions.prompt: A straight position–time segment goes from 2 m at 0 s to 14 m at 3 s. What velocity does it show, in m/s?
hints: Read the changes on both axes.
Divide position change by time change.
Calculate (14 − 2)/3.
questions.onCorrect: +4 m/s. Rise over run on a position–time graph is velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in position only. Divide it by the time the change took.
That divides time by position. The slope is position change per unit time.

questions.prompt: A position–time graph is horizontal from 2 s to 4 s. What does the object do during that interval?
hints: Compare the position at the ends of the horizontal segment.

acceptedIdeas: Stays at the same position
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Position stays fixed during the interval, so the object is stationary.

choices.label: Moves at a positive constant speed

questions.onCorrect: Flat means the position does not change, so the object is at rest during that time.

misconceptions.feedback: Constant speed would need a line that rises or falls. This line stays at one height.
Accelerating would show a curve. A level line means no change in position at all.

questions.prompt: Position falls from 10 m to 2 m along a straight graph segment lasting 4 s. Find the velocity in m/s.
hints: A falling position reading has a negative change.
Use final position minus initial position.
Calculate (2 − 10)/4.
questions.onCorrect: −2 m/s. A falling position line means a negative velocity. Final minus initial, over the time.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the position is falling. The velocity has to be negative.
That is the change in position alone. Divide by the time it took.

questions.prompt: A graph starts at 0 m at 0 s and finishes at 2 m at 6 s, with a pause and reversal between. Find the overall average velocity in m/s; a fraction is accepted.
hints: Use the outer endpoints for the full interval.
Include the entire elapsed time, including the pause.
Divide 2 by 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Overall displacement is 2 m over 6 s: 2/6 = 1/3 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: 1/3 m/s. Use the outer endpoints and the whole time. The pause and the turn still count as time.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the position change by the wrong time. Use the full 6 seconds.
That drops the pause from the time. The time on the graph runs from start to finish.

questions.prompt: A straight graph segment runs from x = 3 m at t = 1 s to x = 15 m at t = 4 s. Find its velocity in m/s.
hints: Subtract the earlier reading from the later reading on each axis.
Subtract the earlier time from the later time.
Divide the change in position by the change in time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Position change is 12 m and time change is 3 s: 12/3 = 4 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: +4 m/s. Subtract on both axes, then divide: the change in position over the change in time.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in position. Divide by the change in time as well.
That divides the later position by the later time. Use the changes, not the readings.

questions.prompt: What does a straight rising line on a position–time graph indicate?
hints: A graph of position against time shows a rate, not the shape of the road.

acceptedIdeas: Constant positive velocity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equal time intervals produce equal positive position changes, which is constant positive velocity.

questions.onCorrect: A straight rising line means equal position steps in equal times: constant positive velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: The graph plots position against time. It does not show the slope of a road.
Increasing velocity would bend the line upward. A straight line has one constant slope.

questions.prompt: A cart changes velocity from 2 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².
hints: Find the signed change in velocity.
Divide that change by the elapsed time.
Subtract initial from final velocity, then divide by duration.
questions.onCorrect: 2 m/s². Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time it took.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in velocity. Divide by the time to get a rate.
That divides the final velocity by the time. Use the change in velocity.

questions.prompt: Velocity changes from −8 m/s to −2 m/s over 3 s. What is the average acceleration in m/s²?
hints: Subtract the initial negative velocity carefully.
The velocity moves toward zero.
Calculate (−2 − (−8))/3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The velocity change is −2 − (−8) = +6 m/s. Dividing by 3 s gives +2 m/s².

questions.onCorrect: +2 m/s². Velocity rose from −8 to −2, so acceleration is positive even though the cart is slowing.

misconceptions.feedback: The cart is slowing, but acceleration is final minus initial velocity. That change is positive.
That adds the two velocities. Subtract the initial from the final.

questions.prompt: A cart has negative velocity and negative acceleration. What happens to its speed while those signs remain?
hints: Compare the directions, rather than interpreting a minus sign as braking.

acceptedIdeas: Its speed increases
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Velocity and acceleration both point left, so the magnitude of velocity increases.

questions.onCorrect: Its speed increases. Velocity and acceleration point the same way, so the cart speeds up.

misconceptions.feedback: A minus sign alone does not mean slowing down. Compare the directions of velocity and acceleration.
Nothing here makes the velocity zero. It only grows in the direction it already points.

questions.prompt: A cart keeps a velocity of 6 m/s for 4 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².
hints: Acceleration depends on a change in velocity.
Compare the initial and final velocities.
Calculate (6 − 6)/4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There is no velocity change: (6 − 6)/4 = 0 m/s².

questions.onCorrect: 0 m/s². Velocity did not change, so there is no acceleration, though the cart keeps moving.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the velocity. Acceleration is how much the velocity changes.
That divides the velocity by the time. Acceleration needs a change in velocity.

questions.prompt: A robot's velocity changes from 9 m/s to −3 m/s in 4 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².
hints: The final velocity points opposite to the initial velocity.
Keep signs when subtracting.
Divide the negative velocity change by elapsed time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The change is −3 − 9 = −12 m/s. Acceleration is −12/4 = −3 m/s².

questions.onCorrect: −3 m/s². The velocity change is final minus initial, and it is negative because the robot reverses.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the velocity falls. The sign has to show that.
That adds the velocities. Subtract the initial from the final.

questions.prompt: A velocity–time line crosses zero with a nonzero slope. At that instant, which description is possible?
hints: Velocity is the graph's height; acceleration is its slope.

acceptedIdeas: Zero velocity with nonzero acceleration
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The graph's value is zero at the crossing, while its slope remains nonzero.

choices.label: Zero velocity must mean zero acceleration

questions.onCorrect: Zero velocity with nonzero acceleration. Height on the graph is velocity; slope is acceleration.

misconceptions.feedback: Velocity is the height of the graph and acceleration is its slope. A line can be at zero height and still slope.
A straight line has one slope throughout. It does not change at the crossing.

questions.prompt: A cart starts at 3 m/s and has constant acceleration 2 m/s² for 4 s. Find its final velocity in m/s.
hints: Find the velocity added during the interval.
Multiply acceleration by time, then add the initial velocity.
Calculate 3 + 2 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: 11 m/s. Constant acceleration adds the same velocity every second: start plus acceleration times time.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds one second's gain only. The cart gains it every second for 4 s.
That is the velocity gained. The cart also started with some velocity.

questions.prompt: Starting at 3 m/s, a cart accelerates at 2 m/s² for 4 s. What is its displacement in metres?
hints: You already have the average velocity from the lines above.
Distance covered is average velocity times time.
Multiply the 7 m/s by the 4 s.
questions.onCorrect: 28 m. Average velocity times time, with the average taken halfway between start and finish.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance if the cart held its starting velocity. It speeds up, so it covers more.
That uses at² without the half. Average the start and finish velocities instead.

questions.prompt: An object starts from rest with constant nonzero acceleration. Doubling the travel time multiplies its displacement by what factor?
hints: Track the exponent on time in ½at².

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Displacement is proportional to time squared; doubling time gives a factor of 2² = 4.

questions.onCorrect: A factor of 4. From rest, displacement grows with time squared, so doubling the time quadruples it.

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling the time also doubles the final velocity, so the distance grows by more than a factor of two.
That would need time cubed. Displacement from rest goes as time squared.

questions.prompt: A cart brakes uniformly from 12 m/s to rest in 4 s. Find its stopping distance in metres.
hints: Uniform braking makes the velocity change linearly.
Average the initial and final velocities.
Multiply (12 + 0)/2 by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Average velocity is (12 + 0)/2 = 6 m/s. Displacement is 6 × 4 = 24 m.

questions.onCorrect: 24 m. Uniform braking makes the average velocity the mean of start and finish; multiply by the time.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the cart as moving at its starting velocity throughout. It slows down, so it goes less far.
That is the average velocity. Multiply it by the time to get a distance.

questions.prompt: A robot begins at x = 5 m with velocity 2 m/s and constant acceleration 1 m/s². Find its position after 4 s, in metres.
hints: First find displacement, then add the initial position.
Use x = x₀ + ut + ½at².
Calculate 5 + 8 + 8.
questions.onCorrect: 21 m. Start position, plus distance from the initial velocity, plus the extra from accelerating.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the extra distance gained by accelerating. Add ½at² as well.
That leaves out the half in ½at². Check the last term.

questions.prompt: When is displacement = ut + ½at² valid for the whole interval?
hints: Identify the assumption used to combine the velocity changes.

acceptedIdeas: When acceleration is constant over the interval
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: This expression assumes constant acceleration during the interval; direction alone is not enough.

choices.label: When acceleration is constant over the interval

questions.onCorrect: Only when acceleration is constant over the interval. That is the assumption the formula is built on.

misconceptions.feedback: Starting from rest is a special case of the formula, not a condition for using it.
The direction of motion does not matter. What matters is that the acceleration stays the same.

questions.prompt: A ball is released from rest. Take upward as positive and g = 10 m/s², with no air resistance. Find its velocity after 2 s, in m/s.
hints: Gravity points opposite to the positive direction.
Use negative acceleration in v = u + at.
Calculate 0 − 10 × 2.
questions.onCorrect: −20 m/s. The ball gains 10 m/s of downward velocity each second, and downward is negative here.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the ball moves down. With upward positive, its velocity is negative.
That is the velocity after one second only. The ball keeps gaining speed for 2 s.

questions.prompt: A ball is released from height 45 m. With g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance, what is its height after 2 s, in metres?
hints: Find the downward displacement from rest.
Subtract ½gt² from the starting height.
Calculate 45 − 0.5 × 10 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: 25 m. Height is the start plus the signed displacement, and falling gives a negative displacement.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the fall to the starting height. The ball goes down, so subtract it.
That uses the distance for 1 s of falling. The ball falls for 2 s.

questions.prompt: At the highest point of a vertical throw, find the acceleration in m/s². Take upward positive, g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance.
hints: Separate zero velocity from zero acceleration.
Gravity continues acting throughout the flight.
Use the downward value of g with upward positive.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Gravity still gives acceleration −10 m/s² at the top; only the instantaneous velocity is zero.

questions.onCorrect: −10 m/s². Velocity is zero at the top for an instant, but gravity keeps pulling down.

misconceptions.feedback: The velocity is zero there, not the acceleration. Gravity still acts at the top.
The size is right, but the pull is downward. With upward positive it needs a minus sign.

questions.prompt: Two objects of different mass are released together from the same height in the same gravitational field. Ignore air resistance. Which lands first?
hints: Check whether mass appears in the free-fall position equation.

acceptedIdeas: They land together
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same initial velocity and gravitational acceleration give the same motion in this model.

questions.onCorrect: They land together. Without air resistance, free-fall acceleration does not depend on mass.

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger weight is balanced by a bigger mass to move. Without air resistance, the two cancel.
Mass does not appear in the free-fall equations. Both objects move the same way.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown upward at 30 m/s. With g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance, find its displacement after 2 s in metres.
hints: Combine the initial upward motion with the downward acceleration.
Use ut − ½gt².
Calculate 60 − 20.
questions.onCorrect: 40 m. Distance from the initial velocity, minus the amount gravity takes back.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores gravity. The ball slows as it rises, so it goes less far than that.
That subtracts the wrong way round. Gravity takes distance off, it does not add.

questions.prompt: While a freely thrown ball is moving upward, which direction does its acceleration point? Ignore air resistance.
hints: The direction of motion does not determine the direction of gravitational acceleration.

acceptedIdeas: Downward, toward Earth
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The gravitational acceleration points downward throughout the flight, including while velocity points upward.

choices.label: Upward, because the ball is rising
It has no acceleration until it falls

questions.onCorrect: Downward, towards Earth. Gravity gives the same downward acceleration on the way up, at the top and on the way down.

misconceptions.feedback: The direction of motion does not set the direction of acceleration. A rising ball is slowing.
Gravity acts the moment the ball leaves the hand, not when it starts to fall.

questions.prompt: Two horizontal forces act on a cart: 14 N right and 6 N left. With right positive, find the net force in newtons.
hints: Give opposite directions opposite signs.
Add the signed forces on the same cart.
Calculate 14 − 6.
questions.onCorrect: +8 N. Net force is the signed sum of the forces on one object, with opposite directions given opposite signs.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes. The leftward force pulls against the rightward one, so subtract.
The size is right, but the larger force points right. The net force is positive.

questions.prompt: A cart is already moving right at 3 m/s. Its net force stays zero. What happens next in an inertial frame?
hints: Balanced forces imply no change in velocity.

acceptedIdeas: It continues at 3 m/s to the right
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero net force leaves the velocity unchanged.

choices.label: It continues at 3 m/s to the right

questions.onCorrect: It keeps going at 3 m/s to the right. Zero net force means no change in velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: Stopping would need a net force opposing the motion. Balanced forces leave the velocity as it is.
Gaining speed would need a net force in the direction of motion. Here it is zero.

questions.prompt: A resting cart has 9 N rightward and 9 N leftward horizontal forces. Find its horizontal net force in newtons.
hints: Compare the two force magnitudes.
Use opposite signs for opposite directions.
Calculate 9 − 9.
questions.onCorrect: 0 N. Equal forces in opposite directions add to zero: balanced forces.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two sizes. The forces point opposite ways, so one takes the other away.
That is one of the two forces. Add both with their signs.

questions.prompt: A cart moving right experiences 8 N right and 20 N left. With right positive, find the net force in newtons.
hints: Separate the velocity direction from the force sum.
The leftward force enters with a minus sign.
Calculate 8 − 20.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 − 20 = −12 N. The net force is leftward even while the cart moves right.

questions.onCorrect: −12 N. The net force points left even though the cart moves right: it slows the cart down.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the larger force points left. The net force is negative.
That adds the sizes. The two forces point opposite ways, so subtract.

questions.prompt: Forces of 7 N and 11 N act rightward on a crate; a 5 N force acts leftward. Find the net force in newtons with right positive.
hints: Group the forces pointing in the same direction.
Add the two rightward forces, then subtract the leftward force.
Calculate 7 + 11 − 5.
questions.onCorrect: +13 N. Add the rightward forces, then take off the leftward one.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the rightward forces are larger. The net force is positive.
That adds all three as if they pointed the same way. The 5 N force points the other way.

questions.prompt: An object moves left at constant nonzero velocity in an inertial frame. What is its net force?
hints: A continuing velocity does not require a continuing net push.

acceptedIdeas: Zero
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Constant velocity means no acceleration, so the net force is zero.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. Constant velocity means no acceleration, so the forces on the object balance.

misconceptions.feedback: A net leftward force would make it accelerate leftward. Its velocity is not changing.
A net rightward force would slow it down. Its velocity is not changing.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg cart has horizontal forces of 18 N right and 6 N left. With right positive, find its acceleration in m/s².
hints: Add the forces before applying the second law.
Divide the net force by mass.
Calculate (18 − 6)/3.
questions.onCorrect: 4 m/s². Add the forces to get the net force, then divide by the mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the net force. Divide it by the mass to get the acceleration.
That divides one force by the mass. Use the net force of both.

questions.prompt: The mass doubles while the net force stays the same. What happens to acceleration?
hints: Keep the numerator fixed in a = F_net/m.

acceptedIdeas: It is halved
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Acceleration is net force divided by mass, so twice the mass gives half the acceleration.

questions.onCorrect: It is halved. The same net force spread over twice the mass gives half the acceleration.

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger mass is harder to accelerate, not easier. Mass is on the bottom of a = F ÷ m.
Mass is in the formula, so changing it changes the acceleration.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart experiences a net force of 24 N rightward. Find its acceleration in m/s² with right positive.
hints: The stated force is already the net force.
Use acceleration = net force divided by mass.
Divide the stated net force by the cart's mass.
questions.onCorrect: 12 m/s². The force given is already the net force, so divide it by the mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies force by mass. To find acceleration, divide the force by the mass.
That subtracts the mass. Divide the force by it.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg cart moving right has forces of 4 N right and 12 N left. With right positive, find its acceleration in m/s².
hints: The velocity does not change the force sum.
Subtract the leftward force and divide by mass.
Calculate (4 − 12)/4.
questions.onCorrect: −2 m/s². The net force is leftward, so the acceleration is leftward whatever way the cart is moving.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the larger force points left. The acceleration is negative.
That drops the 4 N rightward force. Both forces count towards the net force.

questions.prompt: What net force magnitude in newtons gives a 4 kg object an acceleration magnitude of 3 m/s²?
hints: This time, the mass and acceleration are known.
Multiply them to find net force.
Calculate 4 × 3.
questions.onCorrect: 12 N. Net force is mass times acceleration.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides acceleration by mass. To find a force, multiply them.
That adds the two numbers. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A heavier cart and a lighter cart must have the same acceleration. Which needs the larger net force?
hints: Hold acceleration fixed in the second law.

acceptedIdeas: The heavier cart
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: For a fixed acceleration, F_net = ma grows with mass.

choices.label: Both need the same net force

questions.onCorrect: The heavier cart. For the same acceleration, F = ma grows with the mass.

misconceptions.feedback: The lighter cart needs less force for the same acceleration, because it has less mass to move.
Mass sets how much force a given acceleration needs, so the two carts differ.

questions.prompt: An object has mass 3 kg where g = 10 m/s². Find the magnitude of its weight in newtons.
hints: Weight is a force produced by gravity.
Multiply mass by the stated gravitational acceleration.
Calculate 3 × 10.
questions.onCorrect: 30 N. Weight is mass times g: the gravitational force on the object.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mass. Weight is a force: multiply the mass by g.
That adds the mass and g. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg object moves to a location with smaller gravitational acceleration. What happens to its mass?
hints: Mass and weight measure different physical quantities.

acceptedIdeas: It stays 3 kg
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changing the gravitational field changes weight; the object's mass remains 3 kg.

questions.onCorrect: It stays 3 kg. Mass belongs to the object; only the weight changes with the field.

misconceptions.feedback: Mass is the amount of matter, which does not change with place. Weight is what changes.
Weight is a force in newtons and mass is in kilograms. They are different quantities.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg object rests on a horizontal support. Only weight and the upward support force act, with g = 10 m/s². Find the support force in newtons.
hints: At rest, the vertical net force is zero.
The two vertical forces must have equal magnitudes.
Calculate the weight 4 × 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With no vertical acceleration, support balances weight: N = 4 × 10 = 40 N.

questions.onCorrect: 40 N. At rest the net force is zero, so the support force equals the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mass. The support force must match the weight, which is mg.
Gravity is pulling down, so something must be pushing up to keep the object at rest.

questions.prompt: A support accelerates a 4 kg object upward at 2 m/s². Only support and weight act, and g = 10 m/s². Find the support force in newtons.
hints: The support has to balance the weight and also give a net upward force.
Use N = m(g + a).
Add g and the acceleration, then multiply by the mass.
questions.onCorrect: 48 N. The support carries the weight and supplies extra force to accelerate the object upward.

misconceptions.feedback: That only balances the weight. The object is also accelerating upward, which needs more.
That is the extra force for the acceleration alone. The support also carries the weight.

questions.prompt: A 7 kg object is in a field where g = 9.8 m/s². Find its weight magnitude in newtons.
hints: Use the given value of g rather than rounding it to 10.
Multiply mass by gravitational acceleration.
Calculate 7 × 9.8.
questions.onCorrect: 68.6 N. Use the g you are given: weight is mass times g.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds g to 10. The question gives 9.8, so use it.
That divides the mass by g. Weight is mass times g.

questions.prompt: An object on a support moves downward at constant velocity. Only weight and support act. How does the support force compare with weight?
hints: Downward velocity does not imply downward acceleration.

acceptedIdeas: It is equal
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Constant velocity gives zero acceleration, so the support and weight balance.

questions.onCorrect: Equal. Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the support balances the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: A smaller support force would leave a net downward force and the object would speed up downward.
A larger support force would give a net upward force and the object would slow down.

questions.prompt: B pushes A left with a force of 10 N. Find the magnitude of A's force on B in newtons.
hints: Identify the two objects in the interaction.
The two forces have equal magnitudes.
The partner force has the same magnitude and opposite direction.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Newton's third law gives an equal magnitude: 10 N, directed right.

questions.onCorrect: 10 N. The partner force is equal in size and opposite in direction.

misconceptions.feedback: The forces do not cancel here: they act on different objects. Each is the same size.
The two forces have the same size. They are not added together.

questions.prompt: Cart A pushes a 5 kg cart B right with 10 N. This is B's only horizontal force. Find B's acceleration in m/s² with right positive.
hints: Apply the second law to B alone.
Divide the force on B by B's mass.
Divide the interaction force by B's mass.
questions.onCorrect: +2 m/s². Apply the second law to B alone: the force on B divided by B's mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies force by mass. Divide the force by B's mass.
B is pushed right, so its acceleration is positive.

questions.prompt: Cart A has mass 2 kg. Its only horizontal force is 10 N left. With right positive, find A's acceleration in m/s².
hints: Use the mass of the object being accelerated.
The leftward force has a negative sign.
Divide the leftward force magnitude by mass and retain its sign.
questions.onCorrect: −5 m/s². The force on A is leftward, so its acceleration is negative. Divide by A's mass.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but A is pushed left. With right positive, its acceleration is negative.
That multiplies force by mass. Divide the force by A's mass.

questions.prompt: A and B push each other while isolated horizontally. Why do the interaction forces cancel in the combined system's force sum?
hints: Choose a boundary containing both interacting objects.

acceptedIdeas: They are equal, opposite internal forces
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: For the combined system, the pair is internal and sums to zero. Each cart can still accelerate.

choices.label: They act on the same cart
They are equal, opposite internal forces

questions.onCorrect: They are equal, opposite internal forces. Inside the combined system they sum to zero, yet each cart still accelerates.

misconceptions.feedback: The two forces act on different carts, one on each. That is why each cart accelerates.
Each cart has an unbalanced force on it, so both accelerate. The cancelling is only for the pair taken together.

questions.prompt: Two carts interact with forces of magnitude 18 N. Cart B has mass 6 kg and no other horizontal force. Find its acceleration magnitude in m/s².
hints: Use the force acting on B.
Equal interaction forces do not require equal accelerations.
Divide the force magnitude by the mass of B.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s². B's acceleration is the force on B divided by B's mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies force by mass. Divide the force by B's mass.
The forces on the two carts do not cancel. Each acts on a different cart.

questions.prompt: A book rests on a table. Which is the interaction partner of the table's upward force on the book?
hints: A third-law pair acts on different objects.

acceptedIdeas: The book's downward force on the table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The paired force swaps the two objects: book on table, opposite to table on book.

choices.label: Earth's downward gravitational force on the book
The book's downward force on the table

questions.onCorrect: The book's downward force on the table. A pair swaps the objects: table on book, book on table.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a different force on the same book. A pair always acts on two different objects, one force on each.
Mass is not a force. The partner of a force is another force.

questions.prompt: A resting 4 kg box has g = 10 m/s² and static coefficient 0.5. A 12 N horizontal push does not move it. Find the static-friction magnitude in newtons.
hints: A stationary box has zero horizontal acceleration.
Static friction adjusts below its maximum.
Match the applied horizontal push without exceeding the limit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 12 N push is below the 20 N limit, so static friction is 12 N.

questions.onCorrect: 12 N. Static friction adjusts to match the push, as long as the push stays under the limit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the limit, the most static friction can give. Here it only has to match the push.
The box does not move, so something is holding it back. That is friction.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg box rests on a horizontal surface with no other vertical forces. Use g = 10 m/s² and μ_s = 0.5. Find maximum static friction in newtons.
hints: First find the support force.
Multiply mg by the static coefficient.
Calculate 0.5 × 4 × 10.
questions.onCorrect: 20 N. The support force is mg, and the limit is the static coefficient times that.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the support force. Multiply it by the coefficient as well.
That is the coefficient times the mass. Include g: the support force is mg.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg box slides on a horizontal surface. With g = 10 m/s², no vertical acceleration and μ_k = 0.3, find the sliding-friction magnitude in newtons.
hints: Use the coefficient for sliding.
The support force equals mg.
Calculate 0.3 × 40.
questions.onCorrect: 12 N. Sliding friction is the sliding coefficient times the support force.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the static coefficient. A sliding box uses the sliding coefficient.
That multiplies by the mass without g. The support force is mg.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg box slides right. A 24 N push acts right and sliding friction is 12 N left. Find its acceleration in m/s² with right positive.
hints: Combine the opposing horizontal forces.
Divide net force by mass.
Calculate (24 − 12)/4.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s². Subtract the friction from the push to get the net force, then divide by the mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the push alone by the mass. Friction takes some of it away.
That divides the push alone by the mass. Take friction off first.

questions.prompt: A stationary box can sustain at most 30 N of static friction. You push horizontally with 8 N and it stays at rest. What is its friction magnitude?
hints: Use zero acceleration while the box remains at rest.

acceptedIdeas: 8 N
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Static friction balances the 8 N push; 30 N is a limit, not its automatic value.

questions.onCorrect: 8 N. At rest, friction exactly matches the push; the limit is only the most it could give.

misconceptions.feedback: The limit is the most friction can give. It does not set the friction until the push reaches it.
The two do not add. Friction opposes the push, and at rest they balance.

questions.prompt: A sliding box slows to rest on a horizontal floor after its push is removed. What happens next in this model?
hints: Friction opposes sliding or a tendency to slide; it is not a constant backward motor.

acceptedIdeas: It stays at rest with zero horizontal friction
