answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Once sliding stops and no horizontal force tries to move it, friction is zero.

choices.label: It stays at rest with zero horizontal friction
It keeps sliding at a smaller constant speed

questions.onCorrect: It stays at rest with zero horizontal friction. Friction opposes sliding; it does not push backward on its own.

misconceptions.feedback: Friction only opposes sliding. Once the box stops, nothing is trying to move it.
A box that has stopped stays stopped. Friction never starts it moving again.

questions.prompt: A constant 15 N force acts along a 4 m displacement. Find its work in joules.
hints: Force and displacement point the same way.
Multiply their magnitudes.
Calculate 15 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: 60 J. A force along the displacement does positive work: force times distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two numbers. Work is force times distance.
That divides force by distance. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A constant 6 N force acts opposite to a 5 m displacement. Find its signed work in joules.
hints: An opposing force does negative work.
Multiply force and distance, retaining the negative sign.
Calculate −6 × 5.
questions.onCorrect: −30 J. A force against the displacement does negative work: it takes energy away.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the force opposes the motion. Its work is negative.
That subtracts the numbers. Work is force times distance.

questions.prompt: A constant 20 N upward support force acts during a 3 m horizontal displacement. Find the work done by this support force in joules.
hints: Look for the force component along displacement.
The vertical force has no horizontal component.
A zero component gives zero work.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The force is perpendicular to displacement, so its work is 0 J.

questions.onCorrect: 0 J. A force at right angles to the displacement does no work.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the force by the distance. The force is at right angles to the motion, so none of it acts along it.
That is the distance. Work needs a part of the force along it, and there is none.

questions.prompt: A constant 10 N pull acts along a 7 m displacement. Find the work done by this pull alone in joules.
hints: The question asks about one force, not the net force.
Use W = Fd for this parallel pull.
Calculate 10 × 7.
questions.onCorrect: 70 J. The pull's work depends on that pull alone, not on other forces.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the numbers. Work is force times distance.
That divides the force by distance. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: You hold a box stationary for 5 s. What mechanical work does your support force do on the box during that time?
hints: Mechanical work depends on displacement, not the duration of effort.

acceptedIdeas: Zero work because displacement is zero
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The box has no displacement, so this support force does zero mechanical work on it.

choices.label: Zero work because displacement is zero

questions.onCorrect: Zero. Work needs displacement: a force that moves nothing does no mechanical work.

misconceptions.feedback: Time passing does not count. Work needs the object to move along the force.
Gravity does not move the box either. With no displacement, no force does any work.

questions.prompt: A pull does +70 J on a cart and friction does −28 J. All other forces do zero work. What is the net work?
hints: Add work contributions with their signs.

acceptedIdeas: Positive forty-two joules
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Net work is the signed sum: 70 − 28 = 42 J.

questions.onCorrect: +42 J. Net work is the signed sum of each force's work.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes. Friction's work is negative, so it takes away from the pull's.
The pull does more work than friction takes away, so the net is positive.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart moves at 3 m/s. Find its kinetic energy in joules.
hints: Kinetic energy uses speed squared.
Use K = ½mv².
Square the speed, multiply by mass, then take half.
questions.onCorrect: 9 J. Square the speed first, then multiply by the mass and take half.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half. Kinetic energy is ½mv².
That squares the product of mass and speed instead of the speed alone.
That is the speed. Kinetic energy is ½mv².

questions.prompt: A cart's speed doubles while its mass stays fixed. By what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
hints: Mass is fixed, so only the speed term changes.
Doubling the speed doubles v before it is squared.
Square the 2.
questions.onCorrect: 4. The speed is squared, so doubling it multiplies kinetic energy by four.

misconceptions.feedback: That scales energy with speed. Kinetic energy depends on speed squared.
That would be speed cubed. Energy goes as speed squared.

questions.prompt: A cart's mass doubles while its speed stays fixed. What happens to its kinetic energy?
hints: Separate the first power of mass from the square of speed.

acceptedIdeas: It doubles
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mass enters K = ½mv² as a direct multiplier, so energy doubles.

questions.onCorrect: It doubles. Mass multiplies directly in ½mv², so twice the mass is twice the energy.

misconceptions.feedback: More mass at the same speed means more energy, not less.
Squaring applies to the speed, not the mass. Doubling the mass doubles the energy.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart speeds up from 3 m/s to 5 m/s. Find the net work done on it in joules.
hints: Calculate the final and initial kinetic energies.
Net work equals their difference.
Calculate 25 − 9.
questions.onCorrect: 16 J. Net work equals the change in kinetic energy: final minus initial.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the final kinetic energy alone. Net work is the change: final minus initial.
That uses the change in speed. Work is the change in ½mv².

questions.prompt: A 4 kg object moves at speed 5 m/s. Find its kinetic energy in joules.
hints: Square speed before multiplying.
Use the one-half factor.
Calculate 0.5 × 4 × 25.
questions.onCorrect: 50 J. Square the speed, multiply by the mass, take half.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half. Kinetic energy is ½mv².
That uses the speed without squaring it.

questions.prompt: A cart initially has 50 J of kinetic energy and comes to rest. What net work is done on it?
hints: Use the energy change, including its sign.

acceptedIdeas: A loss of fifty joules
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Net work is final minus initial kinetic energy: 0 − 50 = −50 J.

questions.onCorrect: A loss of fifty joules. Net work is final minus initial kinetic energy: 0 − 50.

misconceptions.feedback: The cart lost energy, so the net work is negative, not a gain.
Its kinetic energy changed, so the net work is not zero. Net work equals that change.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg object rises from 1 m to 5 m where g = 10 m/s². Find its gravitational potential-energy change in joules.
hints: Use the difference between final and initial height.
Multiply that difference by mg.
Calculate 3 × 10 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: 120 J. The change is mass times g times the change in height.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the weight. Multiply it by the change in height as well.
That uses the final height instead of the change in height.

questions.prompt: You shift the zero-height reference while describing the same physical rise. What happens to its gravitational potential-energy change?
hints: Only the height difference enters ΔU.

acceptedIdeas: It stays the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both endpoint heights shift equally, leaving both Δh and ΔU unchanged.

questions.onCorrect: It stays the same. Both heights shift together, so the change in height does not move.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing doubles. Both end heights shift by the same amount.
The object really rises, so the change is not zero. Only the labels on the heights move.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg object descends from 8 m to 3 m with g = 10 m/s². Find its signed gravitational potential-energy change in joules.
hints: Final height is less than initial height.
Use final minus initial height.
Calculate 2 × 10 × (−5).
questions.onCorrect: −100 J. The object ends lower, so the change in height and the energy change are negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the object ends lower. Its potential energy falls.
That uses the starting height. Use the change in height: final minus initial.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg object descends from 8 m to 3 m with g = 10 m/s². Find the work done by gravity in joules.
hints: Gravity and this displacement point the same way.
Gravity's work is minus the potential-energy change.
Multiply the weight magnitude by the downward distance.
questions.onCorrect: +100 J. Gravity's work is minus the potential-energy change, so a descent gives positive work.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the potential-energy change. Gravity's work has the opposite sign, and it pulls along the descent.
Gravity acts along the displacement here, not across it, so it does work.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg object rises by 1.5 m where g = 10 m/s². Find its gravitational potential-energy increase in joules.
hints: The height change is already given.
Multiply mass, g and height change.
Calculate 4 × 10 × 1.5.
questions.onCorrect: 60 J. The height change is given, so multiply mass, g and that change.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the weight. Multiply it by the 1.5 m rise as well.
That leaves out g. Multiply mass, g and the rise.

questions.prompt: You assign U = 0 at the floor. Does an object at the floor necessarily have zero kinetic energy?
hints: Height and speed determine different forms of energy.

acceptedIdeas: No, it may still be moving
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The potential-energy reference says nothing about the object's speed or kinetic energy.

choices.label: Yes, all its energy must be zero
No, it may still be moving
Yes, because its height is zero

questions.onCorrect: No. The reference sets where potential energy is zero. It says nothing about the object's speed.

misconceptions.feedback: Potential energy and kinetic energy are separate. A zero height reference only fixes the first.
Height tells you about potential energy only. An object at the floor can still be moving.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg object starts from rest at height 10 m with g = 10 m/s². It reaches zero height with no heating or other energy transfers. Find its final kinetic energy in joules.
hints: The initial kinetic energy is zero.
Use the potential-energy decrease.
Calculate mgh = 2 × 10 × 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Initial potential energy is 2 × 10 × 10 = 200 J; all becomes kinetic energy.

questions.onCorrect: 200 J. With no heating, all the potential energy lost becomes kinetic energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is mg without the height. Multiply by the 10 m drop.
That takes half of the lost energy. With no heating, all of it becomes motion.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg object starts from rest at height 10 m with g = 10 m/s². At zero height, 40 J has become thermal energy and no other transfers occurred. Find its final kinetic energy in joules.

Include the stated thermal energy in the account.
Subtract 40 from 200.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the heating. Some of the energy went into the track instead of motion.

questions.prompt: A descending object loses mechanical energy through friction. The system contains the object, Earth and track, with no external energy transfers. Which sum stays constant?
hints: Follow the energy into the track as well as the object.

acceptedIdeas: Kinetic plus gravitational potential plus thermal energy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Including the thermal energy produced by friction closes the energy account.

questions.onCorrect: Kinetic plus potential plus thermal energy. Include the heating and the account balances.

misconceptions.feedback: Kinetic energy changes during a descent. Only the total of every form stays fixed.
Potential energy falls during a descent. Only the total of every form stays fixed.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg object has final kinetic energy 100 J after a descent. Find its speed in m/s.
hints: Rearrange K = ½mv².

Take the square root of 100.

questions.prompt: An object starts with 12 J of kinetic energy, loses 90 J of gravitational potential energy and produces 18 J of thermal energy. No other transfers occur. Find its final kinetic energy in joules.

Add the potential-energy decrease and subtract heating.
Calculate 12 + 90 − 18.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the heating. Some of the lost energy went into thermal energy.
That adds the heating. Heating takes energy away from the motion.

questions.prompt: With friction, which statement follows for a closed object-Earth-track system?
hints: Distinguish mechanical energy from all the energy forms inside the boundary.

acceptedIdeas: Mechanical energy can decrease while total energy stays constant
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mechanical energy may become thermal energy while the total is conserved.

questions.onCorrect: Mechanical energy can decrease while the total stays constant. It becomes thermal energy.

misconceptions.feedback: Energy is never destroyed. It changes form.
Kinetic energy changes during a descent. Only the total of every form stays fixed.

questions.prompt: A device delivers 1,200 J of useful energy in 4 s. Find its average useful output power in watts.
hints: Power measures energy per unit time.
Divide useful energy by the interval.
Calculate 1,200/4.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies energy by time. Power is energy per second, so divide.

questions.prompt: A device takes in 2,000 J and delivers 1,200 J as useful energy over the same interval. Find its efficiency as a percentage.
hints: Compare useful output with input.
Divide output by input.
Turn the fraction into a percentage by multiplying by 100.
questions.onCorrect: 60%. Efficiency is useful output divided by input energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share that was not useful. Efficiency is the useful share.

questions.prompt: A device takes in 2,000 J, provides 1,200 J of useful output and stores no net energy. How many joules leave through its other outputs?
hints: Account for all the input energy.
Subtract useful output from input.
Calculate 2,000 − 1,200.
questions.onCorrect: 800 J. With no storage, the energy not delivered as useful output leaves through other outputs.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the useful output. Subtract it from the input to find what went elsewhere.
That adds the two. Subtract the useful output from the input.

questions.prompt: A machine delivers the same useful energy in half the time. What happens to its average useful output power?
hints: Keep the energy fixed while changing the denominator.

acceptedIdeas: It doubles
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: P = E/t doubles when E stays fixed and t halves.

questions.onCorrect: It doubles. The same energy in half the time is twice the energy per second.

misconceptions.feedback: Halving the time makes the division give a bigger answer, not a smaller one.
Time is in the denominator, so changing it changes the power.

questions.prompt: A device delivers 350 J of useful output from 500 J input. Find its efficiency as a percentage.
hints: Place useful output on top.
Divide by the input, then multiply by 100.
Divide the output by the input before converting to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 70%. Useful output divided by input, as a percentage.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the wasted share. Efficiency is the useful share.
That divides input by output. Useful output goes on top.

questions.prompt: A device is claimed to deliver more total output energy than all its input energy, with no decrease in stored energy. What must be checked?
hints: Draw the system boundary and account for every energy transfer.

acceptedIdeas: Missing inputs, storage changes or incorrect measurements
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Energy conservation requires all inputs, outputs and storage changes to balance.

choices.label: Only the rate of useful energy delivery
Missing inputs, storage changes or incorrect measurements
Only the fraction of output labelled useful

questions.onCorrect: Check for missing inputs, storage changes or measurement errors. Energy cannot come from nowhere.

misconceptions.feedback: The rate does not fix an energy imbalance. Check where all the energy comes from.
Labelling output as useful changes nothing about the total. Check the energy account.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg cart moves right at 4 m/s. With right positive, find its momentum in kg·m/s.
hints: Momentum is mass times signed velocity.
Use positive velocity for rightward motion.
Calculate 3 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: +12 kg·m/s. Momentum is mass times velocity, and rightward is positive.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the mass and the velocity. Momentum is their product.
The cart moves right, which is positive. So is its momentum.

questions.prompt: A constant net force of 6 N right acts for 3 s. With right positive, find the impulse in N·s.
hints: Impulse combines net force and its duration.
Multiply force by time.
Calculate 6 × 3.
questions.onCorrect: +18 N·s. Impulse is net force times the time it acts.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides force by time. Impulse is their product.
That adds force and time. Impulse is force times time.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg cart initially moves right at 4 m/s. A net impulse of +18 N·s acts. With right positive, find its final velocity in m/s.
hints: Find the initial momentum first.
Add the impulse to it.
Divide the new momentum by the mass.
questions.onCorrect: 10 m/s. Initial momentum plus impulse is final momentum; divide by mass for the velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the impulse by the mass, which gives the change in velocity. Add the starting velocity.
That multiplies by the mass at the end. Divide the final momentum by the mass.

questions.prompt: A cart reverses from +4 m/s to −4 m/s without changing mass. Which endpoint quantity is unchanged?
hints: Compare how velocity enters p = mv and K = ½mv².

acceptedIdeas: Kinetic energy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The speed squared is unchanged, so kinetic energy is the same; momentum and velocity reverse signs.

questions.onCorrect: Kinetic energy. Speed squared is the same either way, while velocity and momentum change sign.

misconceptions.feedback: Momentum carries the sign of the velocity, so it reverses.
The velocity goes from +4 to −4, so it is the thing that reverses.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg cart moving at +6 m/s stops in 3 s. Find the average net force in newtons with right positive.
hints: Stopping reduces the positive momentum to zero.
Divide the signed momentum change by time.
Divide the lost momentum by the stopping time and retain its negative sign.
questions.onCorrect: −8 N. The cart loses 24 kg·m/s over 3 s, so the average net force is negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the force slows a rightward cart. It points left, so it is negative.
That multiplies by the time. Divide the momentum change by it.

questions.prompt: The same object undergoes the same momentum change over a longer stopping time. What happens to the magnitude of its average net force?
hints: Use F_avg = Δp/Δt with a fixed numerator.

acceptedIdeas: It decreases
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The fixed impulse is spread over more time, reducing average force magnitude.

questions.onCorrect: It decreases. The same momentum change spread over more time needs a smaller average force.

misconceptions.feedback: Longer time in the denominator makes the force smaller, not larger.
The time is in the formula, so changing it changes the force.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart at +6 m/s hits a resting 4 kg cart and they stick. External impulse is negligible. Find their shared final velocity in m/s.
hints: Add both initial signed momenta.
The stuck carts have combined mass 6 kg.
Divide 12 by 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Total momentum is 2 × 6 + 4 × 0 = 12 kg·m/s; v = 12/(2 + 4) = 2 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: 2 m/s. Total momentum is conserved, so divide it by the combined mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first cart's velocity. After sticking, the combined mass shares the momentum.
That divides by one cart's mass. Use the combined mass.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart at +6 m/s and a 4 kg cart at −3 m/s collide and stick. External impulse is negligible. Find their shared final velocity in m/s.
hints: Include the negative sign of the second velocity.
Add 12 and −12.
Divide the total momentum by 6 kg.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Initial momentum is 2 × 6 + 4 × (−3) = 0; final velocity is 0 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: 0 m/s. The two momenta are equal and opposite, so the total is zero and the pair stops.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two velocities and halves them. Add the momenta, then divide by the total mass.
The two momenta cancel exactly, so there is none left to give the pair a velocity.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart at 6 m/s hits a resting 4 kg cart. They stick and move at 2 m/s. How many joules of kinetic energy are converted into other forms?
hints: Calculate kinetic energy before and after contact.
Use the combined mass for the final state.
Subtract 12 J from 36 J.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Initial K = ½ × 2 × 6² = 36 J; final K = ½ × 6 × 2² = 12 J; decrease = 24 J.

questions.onCorrect: 24 J. Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not: 36 J before, 12 J after.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the kinetic energy afterwards. The question asks how much was converted.
That is the kinetic energy before. Subtract what is left afterwards.

questions.prompt: What condition justifies conserving the total momentum of two colliding carts?
hints: Separate internal collision forces from external influences.

acceptedIdeas: The external impulse on the two-cart system is negligible
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The total momentum changes by external impulse, so negligible external impulse permits momentum conservation.

choices.label: The carts must have equal mass
The external impulse on the two-cart system is negligible
The carts must conserve kinetic energy

questions.onCorrect: When the external impulse on the system is negligible. Then only internal forces act, and they cancel in the total.

misconceptions.feedback: Equal masses are not needed. Any masses work if there is no external impulse.
Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision. The condition is about external impulse.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg cart at +4 m/s hits a resting 1 kg cart and they stick. External impulse is negligible. Find their shared final velocity in m/s.
hints: Find total initial momentum.
Use the combined mass after sticking.
Divide total initial momentum by the combined mass.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s. Total momentum over combined mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the moving cart's velocity. After sticking, the carts share the momentum.
That is the total momentum. Divide by the combined mass.

questions.prompt: In an isolated sticking collision, what is conserved across the collision?
hints: Apply the conservation rule to the whole system.

acceptedIdeas: Total momentum; kinetic energy may become other forms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Internal forces exchange momentum between carts; total momentum remains fixed while some kinetic energy becomes other forms.

choices.label: Total momentum; kinetic energy may become other forms
Kinetic energy, but not total momentum

questions.onCorrect: Total momentum is conserved. Kinetic energy may become other forms such as heat and sound.

misconceptions.feedback: Each cart's momentum changes in a collision. The total is what stays fixed.
It is the reverse: total momentum is conserved, and kinetic energy is not.

questions.prompt: By how many newtons does the stronger pull win?

Take the 350 away from the 400.
questions.onCorrect: 50 N. The two pulls partly cancel, and what is left decides the direction.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two pulls. They are in opposite directions, so one cancels part of the other.

questions.prompt: A crate has forces of 25 N right and 10 N left on it. With right positive, find the net force in newtons.

Add the two signed forces.

questions.prompt: Why do both leftward forces get a minus sign?

questions.prompt: A rope pulls a block right with 50 N. A second rope pulls it left. The block moves right at a constant velocity. How big is the leftward pull, in newtons?

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart moves at +9 m/s and hits a resting 1 kg cart. They stick together. What is their shared velocity, in m/s?

questions.prompt: Why is the second cart's momentum negative?

Four lots of 3 m/s.

questions.prompt: Why is the acceleration positive when the cart goes from −8 m/s to −2 m/s?

questions.prompt: A cart moving at −10 m/s slows to −4 m/s in 3 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².

Divide the change by 3 seconds.

questions.prompt: The same brakes stop it from 6 m/s in how many metres?

questions.prompt: A 1 kg ball moves at 6 m/s. What is its kinetic energy in joules?

questions.prompt: Why does kinetic energy go up by more than the speed does?

questions.prompt: A cart's kinetic energy rises from 10 J to 25 J. What net work was done on it, in joules?

Net work is final minus initial.

questions.onCorrect: −24 J. The cart loses kinetic energy, so the net work is negative.

questions.prompt: How fast is it going after 5 s, in m/s?
hints: How much speed does it gain in one second?
The gain is the same every second.
Multiply the gain per second by 5.

questions.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest. Take upward as positive, g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance. What is its velocity after 3 s, in m/s?
hints: With upward positive, which sign does gravity's acceleration have?

Multiply the acceleration by 3 s.

questions.prompt: Why is the displacement of a falling ball negative here?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown upward at 25 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s² and ignore air resistance. What is its velocity after 2 s, in m/s? Upward is positive.

questions.prompt: The same push makes an empty trolley speed up by 6 m/s each second. By how much per second will it speed up a trolley loaded to twice the mass?

Twice the mass to move with the same push.
Share the 6 m/s over two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Twice the mass, same push: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 m/s each second.

questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s². The same push on twice the mass gives half the acceleration. That is Newton's second law.

questions.prompt: A net force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg cart. What is its acceleration in m/s²?
hints: Is the force given the net force?
Use acceleration = net force ÷ mass.
Share the 20 N across the 4 kg.
questions.onCorrect: 5 m/s². Acceleration is net force divided by mass.

questions.prompt: Why is 24 N, not 30 N, divided by the mass?

acceptedIdeas: Only the net force counts, so the 6 N leftward force is taken off first.

questions.prompt: A net force of 45 N gives an object an acceleration of 9 m/s². What is its mass in kg?
hints: The second law links force, mass and acceleration.

questions.prompt: How big is the friction force holding it, in newtons?

questions.prompt: A 2 kg box rests on a table with g = 10 m/s² and a static coefficient of 0.6. What is the greatest static friction the table can give, in newtons?

questions.prompt: Why does the crate slide?

questions.prompt: A 6 kg box slides on a floor with μ_k = 0.25 and g = 10 m/s². There is no vertical acceleration. Find the sliding friction in newtons.

questions.prompt: It falls with no air resistance. How many joules of motion energy does it have just before landing?

questions.prompt: A 3 kg block starts at rest and loses 90 J of potential energy while sliding. 30 J becomes thermal energy. What is its final kinetic energy, in joules?
hints: It starts at rest, so it begins with no kinetic energy.
The lost potential energy has to go somewhere.
Subtract the thermal energy from the potential energy lost.
questions.onCorrect: 60 J. Lost potential energy becomes motion plus heating. Take the heating off to find the motion.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the heating. Some of the energy went into the surface.
That adds the heating. It takes energy away from the motion.

questions.prompt: Where did the other 30 J go?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: Into thermal energy of the block and the surface.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Into thermal energy of the block and the surface.

choices.label: Into thermal energy of the block and the surface.

questions.onCorrect: Friction turns mechanical energy into thermal energy. The total stays the same.

misconceptions.feedback: Energy changes form but is never lost.
Then the block would be faster, not slower. The heating takes energy away from its motion.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart has 36 J of kinetic energy. What is its speed, in m/s?
hints: Rearrange K = ½mv² for v.
First find v² = 2K/m.
Take the square root of the result.
questions.onCorrect: 6 m/s. Rearranged: v = √(2K/m).

misconceptions.feedback: That is K divided by the mass. Double it and take the square root.
That is the kinetic energy. Rearrange K = ½mv² for the speed.

questions.prompt: A 1 kg object falls from rest through 20 m with g = 10 m/s². 50 J of its energy becomes heating. What is its final kinetic energy, in joules?
hints: Find the potential energy lost.
Subtract the heating.
Multiply mass, g and the drop, then take off the thermal energy.
questions.onCorrect: 150 J. Potential energy lost, minus the heating, leaves the kinetic energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the heating. Some energy goes into thermal energy.
That adds the heating. It takes energy away from the motion.

questions.prompt: Your lifting force equals its weight, 40 N. How much work do you do, in joules?
hints: You push along the direction of the movement.
Work is force times distance.
Multiply the weight by the height.
questions.onCorrect: 80 J. That work is stored as the box's potential energy: weight times height gained.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the numbers. Work is force times distance.

questions.prompt: A 5 kg object rises 3 m where g = 10 m/s². What is its gravitational potential-energy change, in joules?
hints: The weight is mg.
Multiply the weight by the change in height.
Multiply mass, g and the 3 m.
questions.onCorrect: 150 J. Potential energy change is mgΔh.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out g. Multiply mass, g and the rise.
That is the weight. Multiply it by the rise as well.

questions.prompt: Why is the potential-energy change negative here?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: The object ends lower than it started.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The object ends lower than it started.

choices.label: The object ends lower than it started.

questions.onCorrect: Final height minus initial height is negative, so the potential-energy change is too.

misconceptions.feedback: The mass is unchanged. The sign comes from the change in height.
It can be positive or negative. The sign of the change follows the change in height.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg object rises 2 m with g = 10 m/s². What work does gravity do on it, in joules?
hints: Gravity pulls down while the object moves up.
Work against the movement is negative.
Weight times height, with a minus sign.
questions.onCorrect: −60 J. Gravity's work is minus the potential-energy change. A rise gives negative work.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but gravity pulls down while the object goes up. Its work is negative.
Gravity acts along the vertical movement, so it does work.

questions.prompt: A 5 kg object falls 4 m where g = 10 m/s². What is its gravitational potential-energy change, in joules?
hints: The object ends lower, so the height change is negative.
Multiply mass, g and the signed height change.
Find the weight first, then multiply by the change in height.
questions.onCorrect: −200 J. The object falls, so its potential energy decreases.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the object falls. The change is negative.
That leaves out g. Multiply mass, g and the change in height.

questions.prompt: How far from the door are you, in metres?
hints: Draw the door as 0 and the first walk as a line going out.
The second walk goes back along the same line.
Take the 2 m back off the 5 m.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m. The second walk undid part of the first. Physics keeps track of position this way.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two walks. The second walk goes the other way, so it takes you back towards the door.

questions.prompt: A marker moves from 6 m to 2 m along a track, with right positive. What is its displacement in metres?
hints: Which reading is the finish, and which is the start?
Displacement is the finish minus the start.
Take the 6 away from the 2.
questions.onCorrect: −4 m. It moved towards smaller positions, so the displacement is negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the marker moved the negative way. The sign has to show that.
That adds the two readings. Displacement is a difference: finish minus start.

questions.prompt: A walker goes 4 m right, then 4 m left. What total distance does the walker cover, in metres?
hints: How long is each stretch?
Distance adds each stretch, pointing either way.
Add the two stretches.
questions.onCorrect: 8 m. Distance never cancels: every stretch adds to it, whichever way it points.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the net change in position. Distance counts both stretches.
That is one stretch. The walker covers two.

questions.prompt: Why does the 5 m turning point not appear in the displacement?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: Displacement compares only the start and the finish.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Displacement compares only the start and the finish.

choices.label: Displacement compares only the start and the finish.
The trolley never really reached 5 m.
Turning points are always ignored in physics.

questions.onCorrect: Displacement depends on the two ends only. What happens in between does not change it.

misconceptions.feedback: It did reach 5 m: that is where it turned round. The question is why that point does not enter the sum.
Turning points matter for distance. They are only absent from displacement because of what displacement compares.

questions.prompt: A runner goes from −4 m to 2 m, then on to −3 m. What total distance does the runner cover, in metres?
hints: Break the run at the turning point.
The first stretch is from −4 m to 2 m.
Add 6 and the length of the second stretch.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The stretches are 6 m and 5 m: 6 + 5 = 11 m.

questions.onCorrect: 11 m. Split the run where it turns, then add the lengths of the two stretches.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how far the runner ended from the start. Distance counts the whole path.
That is the first stretch only. Add the stretch back.

questions.prompt: What steady force would stop the same ball over 2 s instead, in newtons?
hints: Is the job the same in both cases?
The same total push is needed, spread over more time.
The time is four times longer, so the force is a fraction of the first.
questions.onCorrect: 10 N. Force times time stays the same, so longer stopping time means a gentler force. That product is called impulse.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the extra time. A longer time needs a smaller force.
The same force for longer would stop more than the ball. A longer stop means less force.

questions.prompt: A 5 kg cart moves left at 2 m/s. With right positive, what is its momentum in kg·m/s?
hints: Momentum is mass times velocity.
Leftward velocity is negative.
Multiply the mass by the signed velocity.
questions.onCorrect: −10 kg·m/s. Momentum carries the sign of the velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the cart moves left. Momentum is negative.
That adds mass and velocity. Momentum is their product.

questions.prompt: Why is the impulse added to the initial momentum?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: Impulse is the change in momentum.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Impulse is the change in momentum.

choices.label: Impulse is the change in momentum.

questions.onCorrect: Final momentum is initial momentum plus the change, which is the impulse.

misconceptions.feedback: Impulse is in N·s, not m/s. It gives the change in momentum.
Impulse adds to momentum or takes from it depending on its sign. It does not always cancel.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart moves at +5 m/s. A net impulse of −6 N·s acts on it. What is its final velocity, in m/s?
hints: Find the initial momentum first.
Add the impulse, with its sign.
Divide the final momentum by the mass.
questions.onCorrect: 2 m/s. A negative impulse takes momentum away, so the cart slows.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the impulse instead of subtracting it. Its sign is negative.
That divides the impulse alone by the mass. Add it to the initial momentum first.

questions.prompt: A 0.5 kg ball moving right at 8 m/s is stopped in 0.2 s. With right positive, what is the average net force on it, in newtons?
hints: Find the momentum change: final minus initial.
The ball starts moving right and ends at rest.
Divide the momentum change by the time.
questions.onCorrect: −20 N. The force acts against the motion, so it is negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the force slows a rightward ball. It points left.
That multiplies by the time. Divide the momentum change by it.

questions.prompt: How hard does B push back on A, in newtons?
hints: Think of pushing a wall. Does the wall push back?
The push back is just as hard.
It has the same size as A's push.
questions.onCorrect: 40 N. Every push has a push back of the same size. That is Newton's third law.

misconceptions.feedback: If B did not push back, A would not be thrown backward. A push always has a push back.
The two forces are the same size, they do not add up to double.

questions.prompt: With right positive, cart A pushes cart B with a force of +10 N. What is B's force on A, as a signed number in newtons?
hints: The partner force has the same size.
It points the opposite way.
Opposite direction means the opposite sign.
questions.onCorrect: −10 N. The partner force has the same size and the opposite sign, and it acts on the other object.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the force on A points the other way. Show that with a sign.
The two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel.

questions.prompt: Why do the carts accelerate differently when the forces are equal?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: Acceleration is force divided by mass, and the masses differ.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Acceleration is force divided by mass, and the masses differ.

choices.label: Acceleration is force divided by mass, and the masses differ.
The heavier cart is pushed harder.
Equal forces only act on the lighter cart.

questions.onCorrect: The forces are equal but the masses are not, so a = F ÷ m gives different accelerations.

misconceptions.feedback: The two forces are equal in size. The difference comes from the masses.
One force acts on each cart. They are equal in size.

questions.prompt: Cart A has mass 4 kg and cart B has mass 8 kg. B pushes A with 16 N to the left. With right positive, what is A's acceleration in m/s²? B's push is A's only horizontal force.
hints: Use the force on A and A's mass.
Leftward means negative.
Divide the signed force by A's mass.
questions.onCorrect: −4 m/s². Use the force on A and A's own mass. B's mass does not enter.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by B's mass. The acceleration of A uses A's mass.
The size is right, but A is pushed left. Its acceleration is negative.

questions.prompt: How many joules does it use each second?
hints: Share the energy equally over the seconds.
The same amount is used every second.
Divide the energy by the time.
questions.onCorrect: 200 J each second. Energy per second is power, and one joule per second is one watt.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies energy by time. Share the energy out over the seconds instead.

questions.prompt: A heater transfers 2,000 J in 5 s. What is its power in watts?
hints: Power is energy per unit time.
Divide the energy by the time.
Share the joules across the seconds.
questions.onCorrect: 400 W. Power is energy divided by time, and one watt is one joule per second.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies energy by time. Divide instead.

questions.prompt: A device takes in 400 J and delivers 100 J as useful output. What is its efficiency, as a percentage?
hints: Compare the useful output with the input.
Divide output by input.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 25%. Efficiency is useful output over input.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the wasted share. Efficiency is the useful share.
That is the input, not the efficiency.

questions.prompt: Why can efficiency never be more than 100%?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: A device cannot deliver more useful energy than it takes in.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A device cannot deliver more useful energy than it takes in.

choices.label: A device cannot deliver more useful energy than it takes in.

questions.onCorrect: Output cannot exceed input, or energy would be created.

misconceptions.feedback: The limit is physical, not arithmetic. It comes from the energy account.
Some energy is wasted, but not all of it. Efficiency is the useful share.

questions.prompt: A machine delivers 120 W of useful power and is 40% efficient. What input power does it need, in watts?
hints: Efficiency is useful output divided by input.
Rearrange to input = output ÷ efficiency.
Divide the output power by 0.4.
questions.onCorrect: 300 W. Input power is useful output power divided by efficiency.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies output by efficiency. Divide instead, since the input is the larger number.
That adds the efficiency as if it were 40 W. Use the fraction 0.4.

questions.prompt: How far does it go, in metres?
hints: It covers the same distance every second.
How far does it go in one second?
Multiply that by the 8 seconds.
questions.onCorrect: 40 m. Steady speed times time gives distance. Next: what to use when the speed keeps changing.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the speed and the time. Distance builds up second by second, so multiply.

questions.prompt: A cart moves at 14 m/s and brakes with acceleration −3 m/s² for 4 s. What is its final velocity in m/s?
hints: Braking has a negative acceleration, so each second takes velocity away.
Find the total change in velocity over the whole time.
Add that change to the 14 m/s start.
questions.onCorrect: 2 m/s. A negative acceleration takes the same amount of velocity away each second.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the velocity change as if the cart sped up. The acceleration is negative, so it takes velocity away.
That is the change in velocity only. Add it to the 14 m/s start.

questions.prompt: Why can the mean of the start and finish velocities stand in for the whole trip?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: Constant acceleration changes the velocity steadily.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Constant acceleration changes the velocity steadily.

choices.label: Constant acceleration changes the velocity steadily.

questions.onCorrect: Steady change means the velocity spends equal time above and below the midpoint.

misconceptions.feedback: The velocity does change, from start to finish. The mean works because it changes steadily.
This cart does not start from rest. The mean works for any steady change.

questions.prompt: A cart at 8 m/s accelerates at 2 m/s² for 3 s. Find its displacement in metres.
hints: Find the final velocity first.
Average the starting and finishing velocities.
Multiply that average by the 3 s.
questions.onCorrect: 33 m. Find the final velocity, take the mean with the start, then multiply by the time.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance at the starting velocity. The cart speeds up, so it goes further.
That uses the final velocity for the whole trip. The cart was slower earlier on.

questions.prompt: How far away are they after 6 s?
hints: How many 2-second chunks fit into 6 seconds?
Each chunk adds the same distance.
Three chunks of 3 m.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 s is three lots of 2 s, so 3 × 3 = 9 m.

questions.onCorrect: 9 m. Equal times give equal steps in position. A straight line on a graph shows exactly that.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the extra time as only 3 m more. Each 2 s adds 3 m, so 6 s adds more than that.
That multiplies the distance by the time. Count how many 2 s chunks fit into 6 s.

questions.prompt: A straight position–time line passes through 4 m at 1 s and 10 m at 3 s. What is its slope in m/s?
hints: How much does the position change between the two points?
How much does the time change?
Divide the position change by the time change.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s. The slope of a position–time line is the velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in position only. Divide it by the change in time.
That reads off a single point. Use the change between the two.

questions.prompt: Why does a flat stretch on this graph mean the object has stopped?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: Its position stays the same while time passes.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its position stays the same while time passes.

choices.label: Its position stays the same while time passes.
Its velocity is at its largest.

questions.onCorrect: The vertical axis is position, not height. A flat line means position is not changing.

misconceptions.feedback: The graph does not show the road. Its vertical axis is position along the track.
The slope of a flat line is zero, and the slope is the velocity.

questions.prompt: A position–time graph has one straight segment from 20 m at 0 s to 5 m at 3 s. What velocity does it show, in m/s?
hints: Is the position rising or falling?
Final position minus initial position, over the time.
Take 20 away from 5, then share it over the 3 s.
questions.onCorrect: −5 m/s. The line falls, so the velocity is negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the position falls. Show that with a sign.
That is the change in position. Divide it by the time as well.

questions.prompt: Cycling at a steady pace, you cover 20 m in 4 s. How many metres do you cover each second?
hints: Share the 20 m equally across the 4 seconds.
Each second covers the same distance.
How many 4s fit into 20?
questions.onCorrect: 5 m/s. Sharing a distance equally over the time taken is the idea behind every speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two numbers. Each second covers less than the whole 20 m, so divide.

questions.prompt: A cart's displacement is −10 m over 5 s. What is its average velocity in m/s?
hints: Which quantity is on the top of the division: distance or displacement?
Divide the signed displacement by the elapsed time.
Keep the minus sign through the division.
questions.onCorrect: −2 m/s. Dividing by a positive time keeps the sign of the displacement.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but velocity carries the direction. The displacement was negative.
That multiplies by the time. Divide the displacement by it.

questions.prompt: Why are the two averages different for this trip?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: The trolley turned back, so the displacement is smaller than the distance.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The trolley turned back, so the displacement is smaller than the distance.

choices.label: The trolley turned back, so the displacement is smaller than the distance.
Velocity is always half of speed.
The times are different for each average.

questions.onCorrect: Turning back shrinks the displacement but not the distance. Same time, different top line.

misconceptions.feedback: There is no fixed ratio. The two averages differ here because of what goes on top of the division.
Both averages use the same total time. Look at the quantity divided by it.

questions.prompt: A walker goes 30 m east in 5 s, then 6 m west in 1 s. With east positive, what is the average velocity over the whole trip, in m/s?
hints: Subtract the westward distance from the eastward distance to get the net move.
Add the two times to get the whole trip's time.
Divide the net move by the total time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Displacement 30 − 6 = +24 m over 6 s gives +4 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: +4 m/s. Net displacement over total time: the westward stretch partly cancels the eastward one.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the whole path length by the time. That is the average speed, not the velocity.
The walker finishes east of the start, so the net movement is eastward.

questions.prompt: How big is the pull on a 6 kg bag, in newtons?
hints: How much pull is there on one kilogram?
Each kilogram has its own 10 N.
Count the kilograms and multiply.
questions.onCorrect: 60 N. Pull per kilogram times the number of kilograms: that is the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the numbers. Each kilogram gets its own 10 N, so multiply.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg object weighs 30 N on Earth. On a planet where g = 4 m/s², what does it weigh, in newtons?
hints: Does the 3 kg change when the object moves?
Weight is mass times g for the new planet.
Multiply the mass by the new g.
questions.onCorrect: 12 N. The mass is still 3 kg. Only g changed, so the weight did.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the weight on Earth. The new planet has a different g.
That adds the mass and g. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A 7 kg box rests on a shelf. Only its weight and the shelf's upward force act, with g = 10 m/s². What is the upward force from the shelf, in newtons?
hints: Is the box accelerating?
Then the net force is zero.
The shelf force must match the weight.
questions.onCorrect: 70 N. With no acceleration, the support force equals the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: The box is not falling, so something is holding it up.
That is the mass. The force is mass times g.

questions.prompt: Why must the support force be larger than the weight here?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: The net force must point upward to give an upward acceleration.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The net force must point upward to give an upward acceleration.

choices.label: The net force must point upward to give an upward acceleration.
The object gets heavier when it moves.
Gravity switches off in a lift.

questions.onCorrect: Net force is support minus weight. For an upward acceleration it has to be positive.

misconceptions.feedback: The weight stays mg. It is the support that changes.
Gravity keeps pulling. The support has to do more than balance it.

questions.prompt: A 6 kg load in a lift accelerates downward at 3 m/s². Only its weight and the support force act, with g = 10 m/s². What is the support force, in newtons?
hints: Upward is positive, so the acceleration is negative.
Use N = m(g + a) with a negative.
Take the acceleration off g, then multiply by the mass.
questions.onCorrect: 42 N. The load accelerates down, so the support force is less than the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: That only balances the weight. The load is accelerating downward, so the support gives less than that.
That treats the acceleration as upward. It points down, so it reduces the support force.

questions.prompt: How many units does the same push cost over 8 m?
hints: How much effort is each metre?
The push is the same, so each metre costs the same.
Multiply the cost per metre by 8.
questions.onCorrect: 80 units. Same push, four times the distance, four times the effort. Physics calls this effort work.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the extra distance to the cost. The cost grows in step with the distance.

questions.prompt: A constant 9 N force acts along a 6 m displacement. How much work does it do, in joules?
hints: Do the force and the displacement point the same way?
Then the work is positive.
Multiply the force by the distance.
questions.onCorrect: 54 J. Work is force times displacement along the force. The joule is one newton times one metre.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two numbers. Multiply them.
That divides force by distance. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: Why is the work done by friction negative?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: Friction points against the displacement.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Friction points against the displacement.

choices.label: Friction is smaller than the push.
Friction does not touch the box.

questions.onCorrect: A force against the displacement does negative work, whatever its size.

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not decide the sign. Direction relative to the movement does.
Friction acts at the surface where it touches. The sign comes from its direction.

questions.prompt: A 12 N pull acts along a 5 m displacement while 9 N of friction acts against it. What is the net work, in joules?
hints: Find the work of each force with its sign.
Friction's work is negative.
Add the two signed works.
questions.onCorrect: +15 J. Add each force's signed work. Friction takes away from the pull's work.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two works as if both were positive. Friction's work is negative.
That is the net force alone. Multiply by the distance to get work.

citations.claim: Displacement is final position minus initial position, and its sign shows the direction. Position is measured from an origin, a place you choose to call zero. You also choose which way is positive.  A move to larger positions is positive. A move to smaller positions is negative.
The dot starts at 2 m and finishes at 9 m. Right is positive. You just used final minus initial: 9 − 2. The plus sign says the dot moved the positive way.

Distance is the total length of the path, so every stretch adds. Displacement only compares the ends. Distance follows the whole path, and it counts the trip back as well as the trip out. Distance has no direction and is never negative.

A trolley goes from 1 m to 5 m, then back to 2 m. Find its displacement and its distance. Displacement uses only the ends: finish minus start. 2 − 1 = +1 m Distance adds the stretches. Out is 5 − 1. 4 m Back is 5 − 2. Add the two. 4 + 3 = 7 m
A cart goes from 1 m to 7 m and back to 1 m. What distance does it cover? The way out runs from 1 m to 7 m. 7 − 1 = 6 m The way back is the same length. 6 m Add the two stretches.

Two students watch the same trip. They measure from different origins, so their readings differ. Moving the origin shifts both readings together. The gap between them is the displacement, and it stays put.
A robot drives along a straight track, then turns round partway. The robot's displacement is only +3 m, yet it covered 13 m. The turn makes the two numbers differ.
Displacement = 9 − 2 = +7 m.
It travels 6 m out and 6 m back, for 12 m.
Both readings increase by 10 m; their difference stays +7 m.
The path has lengths 8 m and 5 m: 8 + 5 = 13 m.
Final minus initial gives −4 − 5 = −9 m, downward.
Its displacement is 1 − (−2) = 3 m. Its distance is 6 + 3 = 9 m.
5 − 2 = 3 m east of the door.
Displacement compares only the start and the finish.
The stretches are 6 m and 5 m: 6 + 5 = 11 m.
The two lengths are 8 m and 5 m, totalling 13 m.

Average speed is distance over time. Average velocity is displacement over time, so it has a sign. Both averages divide by the elapsed time. They differ in the top line: speed uses the distance travelled, velocity uses the displacement.  Speed is never negative. Velocity is negative when the move is in the negative direction.

A rover drives straight for 6 s and covers 18 m. It does not have to go at one pace the whole way. You divided the distance by the time. That is an average: the rover may have been faster and slower along the way.

A trolley goes 15 m right in 3 s, then 5 m left in 2 s. Find both averages. Add the distances and the times. Speed divides the first by the second. (15 + 5) ÷ (3 + 2) = 4 m/s Displacement is the net move, right positive. 15 − 5 = +10 m Velocity divides the displacement by the same time. 10 ÷ 5 = +2 m/s

A cart's displacement is −12 m over 3 s. What is its average velocity? The displacement is negative, so the cart moved left. −12 m The elapsed time is positive. 3 s Divide the displacement by the time.

A runner goes out 10 m from a marker and comes straight back to it. Think about where the runner ends up. The finish equals the start, so the displacement is zero. Distance and displacement part company on a return trip.
A robot covers two equal stretches, but the second takes longer than the first. The whole trip is 12 m in 6 s. The mean of the two stretch speeds is 2.25 m/s, which overweights the faster stretch.
Average speed = 18/6 = 3 m/s.
Average velocity = −12/3 = −4 m/s.
The displacement is zero, so average velocity is 0/5 = 0 m/s.
The whole trip is 12 m in 6 s, giving 2 m/s. The slower section lasts longer.
Only average velocity must be zero, because displacement is zero. The distance travelled is positive.
20 ÷ 4 = 5 m each second.
The trolley turned back, so the displacement is smaller than the distance.
Displacement 30 − 6 = +24 m over 6 s gives +4 m/s.
Average speed = 35/5 = 7 m/s.
Average velocity = −24/8 = −3 m/s.

On a position–time graph, the slope is the velocity. Time runs along the horizontal axis and position up the vertical one. A straight segment rises or falls by the same amount each second.  A steeper line means a faster move. A falling line means a negative velocity.
The line runs from 2 m at 0 s up to 14 m at 3 s. You divided the rise by the run. That quotient is the velocity along the segment.

Read the graph: out for 2 s, stop for 2 s, then back. The first stretch rises from 0 m to 8 m in 2 s. 8 ÷ 2 = +4 m/s The middle stretch is flat, so the position holds. 0 ÷ 2 = 0 m/s The last stretch falls from 8 m to 2 m in 2 s. (2 − 8) ÷ 2 = −3 m/s
Read the graph between 2 s and 4 s, where the line is level. The position at 2 s is 8 m. The position at 4 s is also 8 m. What does the object do?

This segment falls from left to right. Think about what a falling position means for the direction of motion. Final minus initial is negative, so the velocity is negative: motion in the negative direction.

A graph shows a trip with a pause and a turn. Only the start, the finish and the total time matter for the average. The pause and the turn still use up time, so they pull the average velocity down to 1/3 m/s.
The slope is (14 − 2)/(3 − 0) = 4 m/s.
Position stays fixed during the interval, so the object is stationary.
Velocity = (2 − 10)/4 = −2 m/s.
Overall displacement is 2 m over 6 s: 2/6 = 1/3 m/s.
Position change is 12 m and time change is 3 s: 12/3 = 4 m/s.
Equal time intervals produce equal positive position changes, which is constant positive velocity.
6 s is three lots of 2 s, so 3 × 3 = 9 m.
Its position stays the same while time passes.
The slope is (9 − (−3))/4 = 3 m/s.
Velocity = (−4 − 8)/3 = −4 m/s.

Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time it takes. Velocity can change in size, in direction or both. Acceleration measures how quickly.  The unit is m/s², metres per second, every second.
A cart's velocity rises from 2 m/s to 10 m/s over 4 s. You divided the change in velocity by the time. Equal time steps add equal velocity changes when acceleration is constant.

A cart moving left goes from −8 m/s to −2 m/s in 3 s. Find its acceleration. Change in velocity is final minus initial. Subtracting −8 adds 8. −2 − (−8) = +6 m/s The velocity went up towards zero, so the change is positive. Divide by the time. 6 ÷ 3 = +2 m/s²
Velocity goes from −8 m/s to −2 m/s over 3 s. What is the acceleration? Final velocity minus initial velocity. −2 − (−8) Divide by the elapsed time.
A cart moves left and its acceleration also points left. Compare the two directions. Same direction means speeding up. The minus sign does not decide it; the comparison does.
A cart holds 6 m/s for 4 s. It keeps moving the whole time. Velocity did not change, so acceleration is zero, yet the position keeps changing.
Acceleration = (10 − 2)/4 = 2 m/s².
The velocity change is −2 − (−8) = +6 m/s. Dividing by 3 s gives +2 m/s².
Velocity and acceleration both point left, so the magnitude of velocity increases.
There is no velocity change: (6 − 6)/4 = 0 m/s².
The change is −3 − 9 = −12 m/s. Acceleration is −12/4 = −3 m/s².
The graph's value is zero at the crossing, while its slope remains nonzero.
Its velocity increases, from −8 up to −2.

With constant acceleration, final velocity is initial velocity plus acceleration times time. Constant acceleration means the velocity changes by the same amount every second. Write u for the starting velocity, a for the acceleration and t for the time.  A negative a takes velocity away each second.
A cart starts at 3 m/s and accelerates at a steady 2 m/s². Look at how long it runs. You added the velocity gained each second to the starting velocity: 3 + 2 × 4.

A cart starts at 2 m/s and accelerates at 1 m/s² for 6 s. How far does it go? Find the final velocity. 2 + 1 × 6 = 8 m/s Average the start and the finish. (2 + 8) ÷ 2 = 5 m/s Distance is average velocity times time. 5 × 6 = 30 m

A cart starts at 3 m/s and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 4 s. How far does it go? The final velocity is 3 + 2 × 4. 11 m/s The average of the start and finish. (3 + 11) ÷ 2 = 7 m/s Multiply the average velocity by the time.
Brakes can be treated as a constant acceleration. A cart slows steadily until it stops. Same method: the average of 12 and 0 is 6 m/s, and that applies for the whole 4 s.

Now the cart starts from rest and speeds up steadily. Compare the same cart after one time and after twice that time. Doubling the time doubles the final velocity and the average, so the distance grows fourfold.
Displacement = 3 × 4 + ½ × 2 × 4² = 12 + 16 = 28 m.
Displacement is proportional to time squared; doubling time gives a factor of 2² = 4.
Average velocity is (12 + 0)/2 = 6 m/s. Displacement is 6 × 4 = 24 m.
This expression assumes constant acceleration during the interval; direction alone is not enough.
Constant acceleration changes the velocity steadily.

In free fall, everything accelerates at 10 m/s² downward, whatever its mass. Free fall means gravity is the only force acting. Here that means no air resistance. Choose upward as positive and the acceleration is −10 m/s². The sign tells you the direction, nothing else. Rising, at the top and falling: the acceleration is the same.
A ball is released from rest. Upward is positive. You used v = u + at with a = −10. A negative velocity means the ball moves downward.

A ball is dropped from 80 m. How high is it after 3 s? The distance fallen is ½gt². ½ × 10 × 3² = 45 m The ball moves down, so its displacement is negative. −45 m Add the displacement to the starting height. 80 − 45 = 35 m
A ball is dropped from 45 m. How high is it after 2 s? The distance fallen in 2 s is ½gt². ½ × 10 × 2² = 20 m Take that fall off the starting height of 45 m.
Throw a ball straight up. It slows, stops for an instant at the top, then drops back. The velocity is zero at the top but the acceleration is not. Gravity gave −10 on the way up and gives −10 now.

Two balls of different mass leave the same height at the same moment. Air resistance is ignored. Mass cancels: a heavier ball is pulled harder but also has more to move. Free fall is the same for both.
Gravity still gives acceleration −10 m/s² at the top; only the instantaneous velocity is zero.
The same initial velocity and gravitational acceleration give the same motion in this model.
Displacement = 30 × 2 − ½ × 10 × 2² = 40 m upward.
The gravitational acceleration points downward throughout the flight, including while velocity points upward.
It points downward, and upward is positive.
v = 25 − 10 × 2 = +5 m/s, still rising.
With downward positive, v = 0 + 10 × 3 = 30 m/s.

The net force is the sum of the forces on one object, with a sign for direction. Pick the object first. Then give each force a sign: positive if it points the way you chose as positive, negative if it points the other way.  Forces are balanced when the net force is zero. Then the velocity does not change.
Two horizontal forces act on a cart. One points right and one points left. Right is positive. You gave the leftward force a minus sign and added: 14 − 6. The sum points right, so it is positive.

A sled has forces of 12 N right, 7 N left and 3 N left. Find the net force. Give each force its sign, rightward positive. +12, −7, −3 Add them. 12 − 7 − 3 = +2 N The result is small and positive, so the sled's net push is slightly to the right.
A resting cart has 9 N right and 9 N left on it. What is the net force? The rightward force counts as positive. +9 N The leftward force counts as negative. −9 N Add them.
A cart rolls right at 3 m/s. The forces on it add up to zero. Zero net force means no change in velocity, so the cart keeps its 3 m/s. It needs no push to keep going.
A cart rolls right, but the bigger force on it points left. The net force points left while the cart still moves right. The force changes the velocity; it does not show where the cart is going.
Net force = 14 − 6 = +8 N.
Zero net force leaves the velocity unchanged.
9 − 9 = 0 N; the horizontal forces balance.
8 − 20 = −12 N. The net force is leftward even while the cart moves right.
Net force = 7 + 11 − 5 = +13 N.
Constant velocity means no acceleration, so the net force is zero.
400 − 350 = 50 N to the left.
They point opposite to the direction chosen as positive.
Constant velocity means zero net force, so the leftward pull is also 50 N.
An equal opposing force of 14 N makes the net force zero.

Newton's second law: the net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration. The same net force gives a small mass a big acceleration and a large mass a small one. The acceleration points the way the net force points.  Use the net force, not just one of the forces.
A 3 kg cart has two horizontal forces on it, one pointing right and one pointing left. Right is positive. You found the net force first, then divided by the mass. That is the second law at work.

A trolley of mass 8 kg has 30 N right and 6 N left on it. Find its acceleration. Find the net force. The leftward force is negative. 30 − 6 = +24 N Divide the net force by the mass. 24 ÷ 8 = +3 m/s² The sign is positive, so the acceleration points right.
A net force of 24 N pushes a 2 kg cart to the right. Find its acceleration. The force given is already the net force. 24 N The mass is 2 kg. 2 kg Divide the net force by the mass.

A 4 kg cart moves right at 6 m/s. A 4 N force pushes it right and a 12 N force pushes it left. The acceleration follows the net force, not the motion. The cart is still going right, but it is slowing down.
Keep the net force the same and swap the cart for one with twice the mass. a = F ÷ m, so doubling m halves a. Heavier objects respond less to the same force.
Acceleration is net force divided by mass, so twice the mass gives half the acceleration.
For a fixed acceleration, F_net = ma grows with mass.
Twice the mass, same push: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 m/s each second.
Only the net force counts, so the 6 N leftward force is taken off first.

Weight is the gravitational force on an object, W = mg. Mass stays the same wherever you go. Mass is measured in kilograms and belongs to the object. Weight is a force in newtons that depends on g.  On a planet with a different g, the weight changes. The mass does not.
An object has a mass of 3 kg in a place where g is 10 m/s². You multiplied mass by g. The result is a force in newtons, not a mass in kilograms.

A support pushes up on an object. At rest it equals the weight; accelerating upward it is bigger. The support force acts upward on an object resting on a surface or carried in a lift. Take upward as positive: the net force is the support force minus the weight.  At rest, a = 0, so N = mg.

A 2 kg load is carried upward at 3 m/s² in a lift. Find the support force. Take g as 10 m/s². The weight is mg. 2 × 10 = 20 N The net upward force must give the acceleration. 2 × 3 = 6 N The support force carries the weight and supplies the net force. 20 + 6 = 26 N

A 4 kg object is accelerated upward at 2 m/s². Find the support force with g = 10 m/s². The weight is mg. 4 × 10 = 40 N The extra force for the acceleration is ma. 4 × 2 = 8 N Add them to find the support force.
A 4 kg object rests on a horizontal support. Only weight and the support force act. No acceleration means the two forces cancel. The support force has exactly the size of the weight.
Carry the same object to a place with a weaker gravitational field. Weight falls with g, but the mass is the same amount of matter. Mass is not weight.
Changing the gravitational field changes weight; the object's mass remains 3 kg.
With no vertical acceleration, support balances weight: N = 4 × 10 = 40 N.
Constant velocity gives zero acceleration, so the support and weight balance.
The net force must point upward to give an upward acceleration.
Taking upward positive, N = 3 × (10 − 2) = 24 N.

Newton's third law: if A pushes B, B pushes A with an equal force in the opposite direction. The two forces make a pair. They are equal in size and opposite in direction, and they act on different objects. Because each acts on a different object, a pair never cancels on either one.

citations.claim: Static friction matches the push up to a limit. Once the box slides, friction has a fixed size. On a level surface the support force is mg. Static friction can be as large as μs times that, and no larger. Sliding friction is μk times it. Below the limit, static friction equals the push, not the limit.
A 4 kg box can hold at most 20 N of static friction. You push it with 12 N and it stays put. Friction matched your push, 12 N. The 20 N is only the ceiling, not what friction supplies.

A 3 kg crate has μs = 0.4. It is pushed with 15 N on a level floor. Does it slide? Use g = 10 m/s². The support force equals the weight. 3 × 10 = 30 N The most static friction the floor can give. 0.4 × 30 = 12 N The 15 N push beats the 12 N limit, so the crate slides.
A 4 kg box has μs = 0.5. What is the most static friction it can get, with g = 10 m/s²? The support force equals the weight. 4 × 10 = 40 N Multiply by the static coefficient.
The box now slides. Use the sliding coefficient this time. The support force is still mg. Sliding friction is fixed by the coefficient and the support force. It does not grow with the push.
A sliding 4 kg box is pushed right with 24 N while sliding friction pulls left. Net force is push minus friction. That is what accelerates the box: 12 N on 4 kg.
The 12 N push is below the 20 N limit, so static friction is 12 N.
Static friction balances the 8 N push; 30 N is a limit, not its automatic value.
Once sliding stops and no horizontal force tries to move it, friction is zero.
The net force is zero, so friction is 30 N.
The push is bigger than the most static friction can give.
Static friction balances the 9 N push, below the limit.

A force does work when it acts along a displacement: work is force times distance, in joules. Work links a force to a move. Push along the movement and the work is positive. Push against it and the work is negative.  One joule is one newton acting over one metre.
A constant 15 N force acts along a 4 m displacement. You multiplied force by distance, so the work is positive: the force acts along the move.

A box slides 3 m while an 8 N friction force acts against it. Find the work done by friction. Friction points against the displacement, so its work is negative. Multiply force by distance. 8 × 3 = 24 J Attach the sign. −24 J
A 6 N force acts opposite to a 5 m displacement. Find its work. The force opposes the move, so the work is negative. Multiply the force by the distance, with the sign.
Only the part of a force along the displacement does work. A vertical support force acts while the box slides horizontally. The support force has no part along the move, so its work is zero.
Several forces may act on a cart. Work is found for one force at a time. This pull does 70 J. A separate opposing 4 N force over the same 7 m would do −28 J.
The force is perpendicular to displacement, so its work is 0 J.
