citations.claim: Raising an object stores gravitational potential energy: ΔU = mgΔh. Lifting takes work against gravity, and that work is stored. Δh is the final height minus the initial height, so a fall gives a negative change.
A 3 kg object is raised from 1 m to 5 m. Take g as 10 m/s². You found the height change first, then multiplied by mg: 4 m of rise gave 120 J.

A 4 kg object falls from 9 m to 2 m with g = 10 m/s². Find its potential-energy change. The height change is final minus initial. 2 − 9 = −7 m The weight is mg. 4 × 10 = 40 N Multiply the weight by the height change. 40 × (−7) = −280 J
A 2 kg object descends from 8 m to 3 m with g = 10 m/s². Find its potential-energy change. The height change is final minus initial. 3 − 8 = −5 m Multiply mass, g and the height change.

The work gravity does is minus the change in potential energy. Gravity pulls down. When an object goes down, gravity helps the movement and does positive work. When it goes up, gravity opposes it and does negative work.
The same 2 kg object descends from 8 m to 3 m. Use the sign of the energy change you found. A fall lowers potential energy by 100 J, so gravity did +100 J of work.
Two people describe the same rise. One measures height from the floor, the other from the table. Both readings of height shift together, so the difference, and the energy change, agree.
Both endpoint heights shift equally, leaving both Δh and ΔU unchanged.
Gravity does W = −ΔU = −(−100) = +100 J.
The potential-energy reference says nothing about the object's speed or kinetic energy.
The object ends lower than it started.
Gravity does positive work along the descent: 2 × 10 × 4 = 80 J.

Energy changes form but the total of every form stays fixed. Count the object, Earth and the surface as one system. As an object descends, potential energy falls. It becomes kinetic energy and, with friction, thermal energy.
A 2 kg object starts from rest at a height of 10 m with g = 10 m/s². Nothing but gravity does work. All the potential energy lost, 2 × 10 × 10, became kinetic energy.

A 2 kg block slides down from 4 m with g = 10 m/s². 30 J becomes heating. Find its final kinetic energy. Potential energy lost. 2 × 10 × 4 = 80 J Some of it heats the surface. 30 J The rest becomes kinetic energy. 80 − 30 = 50 J
A 2 kg object drops from 10 m with g = 10 m/s². 40 J becomes heating. Find the final kinetic energy. Potential energy lost. 2 × 10 × 10 = 200 J Take off the thermal energy.
Kinetic energy gives speed through v = √(2K/m). Once you know the final kinetic energy, rearrange K = ½mv² to find how fast the object moves.
A 2 kg object ends a descent with some kinetic energy. Work out its speed. With 100 J and 2 kg, v² is 100 and v is 10 m/s.

An object slides down a rough track. The object, Earth and track are one system with nothing else acting on it. Include the heating and the books balance: kinetic plus potential plus thermal never changes.
Initial potential energy is 2 × 10 × 10 = 200 J; all becomes kinetic energy.
Including the thermal energy produced by friction closes the energy account.
Mechanical energy may become thermal energy while the total is conserved.
All 50 J of stored energy becomes motion energy.
Into thermal energy of the block and the surface.
Power is energy transferred per second. One watt is one joule per second. Power says how fast energy is moving, not how much. The same energy delivered in less time is more power.
A device delivers 1,200 J of useful energy in 4 s. You divided the energy by the time: 1,200 ÷ 4 gives 300 joules each second, 300 W.
Efficiency is the useful output energy divided by the input energy. Not all the input does the job you want. The rest leaves as heat, sound or similar. Efficiency is the useful share.

A motor takes in 500 J and delivers 400 J of useful output. Find its efficiency and the wasted energy. Useful output over input. 400 ÷ 500 = 0.8, so 80% The rest leaves through other outputs. 500 − 400 = 100 J
A device takes in 2,000 J and delivers 1,200 J of useful output. Find its efficiency. Divide useful output by input. 1,200 ÷ 2,000 = 0.6 Turn the fraction into a percentage.
The same device stores no net energy. Everything that is not useful output must leave another way. The input of 2,000 J less the 1,200 J of useful output leaves 800 J as heat, sound or similar.
A machine now delivers the same useful energy as before, but in half the time. Power doubles because the same energy takes half as long. The efficiency has not been shown to change.
Other outputs = 2,000 − 1,200 = 800 J.
P = E/t doubles when E stays fixed and t halves.
Energy conservation requires all inputs, outputs and storage changes to balance.
600 ÷ 3 = 200 J each second.
A device cannot deliver more useful energy than it takes in.
Momentum is mass times velocity, and its sign shows the direction. A heavy or fast object has a lot of momentum. Unlike kinetic energy, momentum can be negative: it follows the sign of the velocity.
A 3 kg cart moves right at 4 m/s. Right is positive. You multiplied the mass by the signed velocity. The plus sign comes from the direction of motion.
Impulse is force times time, and it equals the change in momentum. A net force acting for a time changes the momentum. The product is called impulse.

A 2 kg cart moves at +3 m/s. A 5 N net force acts for 4 s. Find its final velocity. Initial momentum. 2 × 3 = +6 kg·m/s Impulse is force times time. Add it to the momentum. 6 + 5 × 4 = 26 kg·m/s Divide by the mass. 26 ÷ 2 = +13 m/s
A 3 kg cart moves at +4 m/s. A net impulse of +18 N·s acts. Find its final velocity. Initial momentum. 3 × 4 = 12 kg·m/s Add the impulse. 12 + 18 = 30 kg·m/s Divide by the mass.
A 2 kg cart moves right and a negative impulse acts on it. Keep the sign when you add it to the momentum. A negative impulse subtracted momentum, so the cart slowed but kept moving right.
A 2 kg cart reverses from +4 m/s to −4 m/s. Compare what changes and what does not. Speed squared is the same, so kinetic energy is too. Momentum changes by −16 kg·m/s because it carries the sign.
p_final = 3 × 4 + 18 = 30 kg·m/s; v_final = 30/3 = 10 m/s.
The speed squared is unchanged, so kinetic energy is the same; momentum and velocity reverse signs.
The fixed impulse is spread over more time, reducing average force magnitude.
Impulse is the change in momentum.

When carts stick, total momentum is conserved and the carts share one velocity. Add each cart's momentum, mass times signed velocity. Afterwards the two masses move together.  This holds when the external impulse on the two carts is negligible.
A 2 kg cart at +6 m/s hits a resting 4 kg cart and they stick. You added the momenta to get 12 kg·m/s, then divided by the combined mass.

A 3 kg cart at +4 m/s and a 1 kg cart at −8 m/s collide and stick. Find their shared velocity. Momentum of the first cart. 3 × 4 = +12 kg·m/s Momentum of the second cart. 1 × (−8) = −8 kg·m/s Add them and divide by the total mass. (12 − 8) ÷ 4 = +1 m/s

A 2 kg cart at +6 m/s and a 4 kg cart at −3 m/s collide and stick. Find their shared velocity. Momentum of the first cart. 2 × 6 = +12 kg·m/s Momentum of the second cart. 4 × (−3) = −12 kg·m/s Add them and divide by the total mass.

A sticking collision conserves momentum but not kinetic energy. Some kinetic energy becomes deformation, heat and sound. A collision like this is called inelastic. Momentum before equals momentum after. Kinetic energy afterwards is less.

A 2 kg cart at 6 m/s hits a resting 4 kg cart. They stick and move at 2 m/s. Find the kinetic energy before and after. From 36 J to 12 J: two thirds of the kinetic energy became other forms, yet momentum was conserved.
Forces between the carts during the crash are internal to the system. Other forces could act from outside. Internal forces cancel in the total, so only a significant external impulse could change it.

Initial K = ½ × 2 × 6² = 36 J; final K = ½ × 6 × 2² = 12 J; decrease = 24 J.
The total momentum changes by external impulse, so negligible external impulse permits momentum conservation.
Internal forces exchange momentum between carts; total momentum remains fixed while some kinetic energy becomes other forms.
Same momentum, twice the mass: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 m/s.
It moves in the negative direction.
Before: ½ × 1 × 16 = 8 J. After: ½ × 2 × 4 = 4 J. Lost: 4 J.
